items.title: Describe the timing rules for elective surgery after coronary stenting.
items.sub: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.eyebrow: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.q: Describe the timing rules for elective surgery after coronary stenting.
items.a:
- Bare metal stent: minimum 4 to 6 weeks of DAPT, then elective surgery with aspirin continued.
- Drug-eluting stent in stable disease: DAPT at least 6 months (3 months for selected new-generation DES in high bleeding risk, ESC), 6 months is the common elective threshold.
- After ACS: 12 months of DAPT; defer elective surgery for 12 months where possible.
- Balloon angioplasty without stent: 2 weeks.
- Time-critical surgery: continue aspirin, stop P2Y12 inhibitor, bridge with cangrelor in the highest-risk stents.
- Stent thrombosis risk factors: early cessation, ACS, long or overlapping stents, left main, bifurcation, low EF, diabetes.

> **Closing point:** Keep aspirin; premature DAPT cessation is the largest driver of stent thrombosis.

items.title: 18. Pulmonary oedema during anaesthesia
items.q: Frothy pink fluid appears in the endotracheal tube 40 minutes into a general anaesthetic with falling SpO2. Describe your immediate management and the differential.
items.a:
## 1. Immediate response
- State the problem aloud and call for help. Ask the surgeon to stop or limit surgical stimulation if the patient is unstable.
- Increase FiO2 to 100%, hand-ventilate to assess compliance, listen to the chest, check the capnogram, SpO2 and airway pressures.
- Confirm tube position (depth, kinking, cuff, endobronchial migration, blockage), the circuit and the ventilator. Suction the tube. Disconnect from the ventilator if a circuit problem is suspected.
- Frothy pink sputum in the tube is a hallmark of severe pulmonary oedema, usually with falling compliance, rising airway pressure and desaturation.

## 2. Initial treatment of hypoxia
- Increase PEEP (start at 8 to 10 cmH2O and titrate to oxygenation and haemodynamics), and consider recruitment manoeuvres cautiously because of haemodynamic effects.
- Maintain adequate ventilation (tidal volume 6 to 8 mL/kg PBW, plateau pressure below 30).
- Stop fluids and any irrigation fluid absorption (hysteroscopy, TURP, arthroscopy, laparoscopic surgery with pressure).
- Treat bronchospasm if present.

## 3. Differential diagnosis and how to separate causes
| Cause | Clues | Quick tests |
|---|---|---|
| Cardiogenic (ischaemia, arrhythmia, valve failure, LV failure) | ST change, hypotension, arrhythmia, high filling pressure, known heart disease | ECG with ST analysis, TOE for new RWMA or valve problem, BNP, PAOP |
| Fluid overload or irrigation absorption (TURP syndrome, hysteroscopy) | Volume balance, hyponatraemia, glycine toxicity, visual changes | Sodium, osmolality, fluid balance |
| Negative pressure oedema | Preceding laryngospasm or obstruction, young fit patient | History, airway events |
| Aspiration | Witnessed regurgitation, bronchospasm | Suction, bronchoscopy |
| Anaphylaxis | Hypotension, bronchospasm, flushing, rash | Tryptase, drug exposure |
| Transfusion reaction (TRALI, TACO) | Recent blood products, fever, hypotension | BNP, response to diuresis |
| Pulmonary embolism (air, thrombus, fat, amniotic) | Falling ETCO2, hypotension, RV strain | TOE |
| Pneumothorax | Unilateral signs, high pressures | Ultrasound, decompression |
| Sepsis or ARDS | Fever, source, vasodilation | Cultures, lactate |

## 4. Treatment according to cause
- **Ischaemia or LV failure:** treat as per R5 and R14; GTN if BP allows, diuretic (furosemide 20 to 40 mg IV), inotrope if low output, vasopressors to protect the coronary perfusion pressure, and consider IABP.
- **Arrhythmia:** synchronised cardioversion if unstable, amiodarone for rate control.
- **Hypertension:** GTN, labetalol.
- **Anaphylaxis:** adrenaline 50 to 100 micrograms IV titrated, fluids, stop the trigger.
- **TRALI / TACO:** stop the transfusion, supportive care, diuretic for TACO only.
- **Fluid overload:** stop infusions, diurese; renal replacement if oliguric.
- **NPPE:** PEEP, supportive; resolution within 24 to 48 hours.

## 5. Anaesthetic and surgical management
- Discuss with the surgeon to finish quickly or abandon.
- Maintain anaesthesia with a technique that minimises myocardial depression.
- Place an arterial line, send ABG, and consider TOE.

## 6. Postoperative care
ICU or HDU, ongoing ventilation or CPAP, serial ECG, troponin and echo, review of fluid balance, and communication with the patient and family (open disclosure, if there was an incident). Document the event and report if a transfusion or drug reaction is suspected.

> **Examiner lens:** airway and oxygenation first, then cause-directed therapy.

items.title: 14. Acute decompensated heart failure on the ICU
items.q: A patient with known cardiomyopathy is admitted with pulmonary oedema, BP 90/60, cool peripheries and rising lactate. Outline your assessment and stepwise management.
items.a:
## 1. Haemodynamic profile and initial assessment
- Hypotension, cool peripheries and rising lactate indicate low output (cold) with pulmonary congestion (wet): the cold and wet profile (Stevenson) carrying the highest mortality, and approaching or in cardiogenic shock (SCAI stage B to C).
- Immediate assessment: ABC, SpO2, respiratory effort, BP, perfusion (capillary refill, lactate, urine output, mentation), JVP, auscultation, and a bedside echo and lung ultrasound.

## 2. Searching for the precipitant (CHAMP)
- **C** oronary syndromes (ACS, ischaemia); **H** ypertensive emergency; **A** rrhythmia (AF with rapid rate, VT, bradycardia) or acute valve failure; **M** echanical complication (papillary rupture, VSD, tamponade); **P** ulmonary embolism.
- Others: sepsis, anaemia, thyroid disease, drugs (NSAIDs, negative inotropes, steroids, chemotherapy), non-adherence, dietary salt, renal failure, alcohol, myocarditis.
- Investigations: 12-lead ECG, troponin, BNP or NT-proBNP, electrolytes, renal and liver function, lactate, ABG, CXR, lung ultrasound (B-lines), echo, and cultures if septic.

## 3. Respiratory support
- Oxygen to SpO2 94 to 98% (or 88 to 92% if CO2 retention).
- CPAP or NIV for respiratory distress: 3CPO (1069 patients) showed faster improvement in dyspnoea and acidosis, but no difference in 7 day mortality between NIV, CPAP and oxygen alone. Care is needed in cardiogenic shock and with haemodynamic compromise because of reduced venous return.
- Intubate for exhaustion, refractory hypoxia, acidosis, depressed consciousness or inability to protect the airway, with a vasopressor running and a titrated induction (see R10).

## 4. Restore perfusion first
- MAP target of 65 mmHg: noradrenaline (first line).
- Low output: dobutamine (2.5 to 10 micrograms/kg/min) or milrinone (0.25 to 0.5 micrograms/kg/min without bolus; reduced dose in renal impairment); levosimendan as an alternative.
- Avoid vasodilators (GTN, nitroprusside) while hypotensive; avoid beta-blockers and negative inotropes.

## 5. Decongestion
- IV loop diuretic (furosemide 40 to 80 mg bolus, or 1 to 2.5 times the oral dose). Check response at 2 hours (spot urine sodium above 50 to 70 mmol/L, urine output above 100 to 150 mL/h).
- Diuretic resistance: increase the dose, infusion, add a thiazide (metolazone) or acetazolamide (ADVOR), or SGLT2 inhibitor.
- DOSE trial: no difference between bolus and infusion, or between low and high dose, in symptoms and renal function, although high dose gave more diuresis.
- Ultrafiltration or renal replacement for refractory overload or oliguric renal failure.

## 6. Mechanical circulatory support
If refractory shock despite inotropes: IABP, Impella or VA-ECMO as a bridge to recovery, device or transplant (see R8).

## 7. Other management
- Treat arrhythmia: synchronised cardioversion for unstable AF or VT, amiodarone; correct potassium and magnesium.
- Anticoagulation for AF or LV thrombus, VTE prophylaxis.
- Monitor for cardiorenal syndrome: creatinine, potassium; avoid nephrotoxins.
- PA catheter: ESCAPE (433 patients) showed no routine benefit; useful for unclear shock, for guiding therapy in refractory cases, or for advanced therapy selection.
- Nutrition, glucose, and treatment of the underlying cause.

## 8. Transition
Once stable, introduce GDMT before discharge (beta-blocker, ACEi/ARNI, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor; STRONG-HF showed benefit of rapid up-titration), and specialist follow-up within 7 to 14 days.

## 9. Key principle
In the cold and wet patient, restore perfusion before decongestion; vasodilators and diuretics may worsen hypotension and renal function.

> **Examiner lens:** in the cold and wet patient, perfusion comes before decongestion.

items.title: For a patient with IHD going to major surgery, state which cardiac drugs you continue and which you withhold.
items.sub: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.eyebrow: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.q: For a patient with IHD going to major surgery, state which cardiac drugs you continue and which you withhold.
items.a:
- Continue: beta-blockers (do not withdraw), statins, aspirin (secondary prevention or stent), calcium channel blockers, nitrates.
- Consider withholding: ACEi/ARB on the day of major surgery (hypotension), diuretics on the morning, SGLT2 inhibitors for 3 to 4 days.
- Do not start on the day of surgery: high-dose beta-blocker (POISE), clonidine (POISE-2), aspirin for primary prevention.
- Anticoagulants: per indication, with bridging only for high-risk states.
- Restart early after surgery.

> **Closing point:** Abrupt withdrawal of beta-blockers, clonidine and statins is harmful.

items.title: State the six RCRI predictors and what the score means.
items.sub: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.eyebrow: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.q: State the six RCRI predictors and what the score means.
items.a:
- High-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, suprainguinal vascular).
- Ischaemic heart disease.
- Heart failure history.
- Cerebrovascular disease (stroke or TIA).
- Insulin-treated diabetes.
- Creatinine above 177 micromol/L (2 mg/dL).
- Interpretation: 0, 1, 2, 3 or more points give a steeply rising risk of major cardiac events (about 3.9, 6.0, 10.1 and 15% in updated data); 2 or more is elevated risk.

> **Closing point:** RCRI is a risk estimate, not a decision tool; it underestimates risk in vascular surgery.

items.title: How do you tell cardiogenic from non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema?
items.sub: 5. Acute pulmonary oedema
items.eyebrow: 5. Acute pulmonary oedema
items.q: How do you tell cardiogenic from non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema?
items.a:
- Clinical: history of heart disease, orthopnoea, S3, raised JVP, warm versus cold.
- CXR: cardiogenic has cardiomegaly, vascular redistribution, septal lines, bat-wing hilar shadows, effusions; non-cardiogenic has peripheral patchy shadows with normal heart size.
- BNP: above 400 pg/mL favours cardiogenic; below 100 argues against.
- Echo: low EF, valve disease, high E/e'.
- PAOP: above 18 mmHg cardiogenic; below 18 non-cardiogenic (Berlin ARDS criteria do not need PAOP).
- Treatment response: rapid improvement with diuresis suggests cardiogenic.

> **Closing point:** Coexistence is common, so use echo and BNP together.

items.title: 23. Linking anatomy, ECG and echo for ischaemia
items.q: During a case you see new ST elevation in the inferior leads with hypotension. Link the likely vessel, the echo view and the segments you would examine, and the associated complications.
items.a:
## 1. From ECG to vessel
- ST elevation in II, III and aVF indicates an inferior infarct. The culprit is the RCA in about 80% of cases (right-dominant circulation), and the circumflex in the remaining 20% (left-dominant or co-dominant).
- Distinguish the culprit: ST elevation in III greater than in II, with ST depression in I and aVL, favours the RCA; ST elevation in II greater than III with lateral extension (V5 to V6) favours the circumflex. Right-sided leads (V4R) showing ST elevation of 1 mm or more confirm RV involvement and a proximal RCA lesion.
- Posterior extension: tall R waves and ST depression in V1 to V3 (confirm with V7 to V9).

## 2. Anatomy of the RCA and its supply
- Origin from the right sinus of Valsalva, running in the right AV groove. Branches: conus branch, SA nodal branch (in 60%), acute marginal branches (RV free wall), AV nodal branch (in 80% of right-dominant hearts, arising at the crux), posterior descending artery (PDA) and posterolateral branches.
- Territory: the RV free wall, the inferior wall of the LV, the posterior third of the interventricular septum, the posteromedial papillary muscle (single supply), and the SA and AV nodes.
- Dominance: right-dominant in about 85% (PDA from the RCA), left-dominant in about 8% (PDA from the circumflex), and co-dominant in the remainder.

## 3. Echo views and segments
| View | Segments seen | Use in this case |
|---|---|---|
| TOE transgastric mid short-axis (TG mid SAX) | All six mid-ventricular segments, at the papillary muscle level: anterior, anteroseptal, inferoseptal, inferior, inferolateral, anterolateral; the three territories in one view (LAD anterior and anteroseptal, RCA inferior and inferoseptal, circumflex inferolateral and anterolateral). Also shows the papillary muscles and RV | The best view for monitoring ischaemia and fluid status; examine inferior and inferoseptal hypokinesis |
| Mid-oesophageal four-chamber | Inferoseptal and anterolateral walls, RV size and function, tricuspid valve | RV dilation and function (TAPSE, S'), septal movement |
| Mid-oesophageal two-chamber | Anterior and inferior walls | Inferior wall abnormality |
| Mid-oesophageal long axis | Anteroseptal and inferolateral walls, LVOT, aortic valve | Posterior wall, MR jet |
| TTE subcostal / apical | Same segments from below | IVC, RV |

Use the 17-segment AHA model and rate each segment as normal, hypokinetic, akinetic or dyskinetic, and compare thickening (not just endocardial excursion). A new RWMA is an early sign of ischaemia, preceding ECG change.

## 4. Associated complications and implications
- **RV infarction** (in 30 to 50% of inferior MIs): hypotension with clear lungs and raised JVP; the RV is preload dependent, so give fluid (250 mL boluses), avoid nitrates, diuretics and other vasodilators, maintain sinus rhythm and AV synchrony, and support with inotropes (dobutamine) if needed. Early reperfusion improves RV function.
- **Bradyarrhythmia and AV block:** the RCA supplies the sinus and AV nodes; atropine, temporary pacing (transvenous or transcutaneous), and a Bezold-Jarisch reflex (vagal) in the first hours are frequent and often self-limited.
- **Papillary muscle rupture:** posteromedial papillary muscle rupture from inferior MI, see R9.
- **Inferior VSR and free wall rupture** are less common than anterior.
- **Arrhythmia:** VF early; AF from atrial ischaemia.

## 5. Management in theatre
- Confirm the finding, treat triggers (see R5), and give oxygen only if hypoxic.
- Support perfusion pressure with noradrenaline or vasopressin and cautious fluid in the setting of RV infarct.
- Obtain a 12-lead ECG with V4R and V7 to V9, and TOE.
- Call cardiology for emergency PCI; manage antithrombotic therapy with the surgeon.
- Treat bradycardia (atropine, pacing), avoid nitrates and vasodilators.
- Move to ICU or cath lab after stabilisation.

## 6. Link the dots
ECG leads identify the territory, territory identifies the vessel, vessel identifies the structures it supplies (RV, nodes, papillary muscle), and those structures predict the complications and guide the echo view that confirms the diagnosis.

> **Examiner lens:** connect the ECG leads to the vessel, the vessel to the structures it supplies, and the structures to the echo view.

items.title: Describe MS and the haemodynamic goals.
items.sub: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.eyebrow: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.q: Describe MS and the haemodynamic goals.
items.a:
- Cause: rheumatic in most; severe MS has area below 1.5 cm2 and pressure half-time 150 ms or more.
- Physiology: fixed obstruction between LA and LV, high LA pressure, pulmonary hypertension, AF with atrial thrombus, small LV preload.
- Goals: slow heart rate (long diastole for LV filling), preserve sinus rhythm or control AF rate, avoid hypovolaemia and fluid overload.
- Maintain SVR; avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia and acidosis, which raise PVR and strain the RV.
- Treat AF rapidly (cardiovert if unstable; beta-blocker, digoxin, amiodarone for rate).
- Anticoagulate AF; DOACs are not recommended in rheumatic MS (INVICTUS).

> **Closing point:** Tachycardia is the enemy, because diastolic filling time is everything.

items.title: 21. Cardiac implantable devices in the perioperative period
items.q: A patient with cardiomyopathy and an ICD with CRT needs bowel surgery using monopolar diathermy. How do you plan?
items.a:
## 1. Why devices matter
Cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) include pacemakers, ICDs and CRT systems (CRT-P and CRT-D). Electromagnetic interference (EMI) from monopolar diathermy can cause oversensing, which inhibits pacing (and a pacing-dependent patient may become asystolic), triggers inappropriate ICD shocks, or causes electrical reset. Other sources include radiofrequency ablation, MRI, lithotripsy, nerve stimulators and cardioversion. Risk is greatest when diathermy is monopolar, used above the umbilicus, in long bursts, and when the patient is pacing-dependent.

## 2. Preoperative assessment
- **Identify the device:** type (pacemaker, ICD, CRT), manufacturer and model, indication, date of implantation, and whether the patient is pacemaker-dependent (underlying rhythm absent or inadequate; ask about syncope history, and check the ECG for a paced rhythm).
- **Last interrogation:** a pacemaker should have been checked within 12 months, and an ICD or CRT within 6 months. If out of date or the device has been affected by an event, obtain interrogation by the cardiac physiologist before elective surgery. Check battery, lead function, programmed rate, and ICD therapies.
- **Plan with the cardiologist or device clinic:** reprogramming, magnet use, who attends, and where the device will be rechecked.
- **Surgical considerations:** site (above or below the umbilicus), diathermy type, other equipment, positioning, and the need for cardioversion.
- **Cardiomyopathy assessment:** EF, symptoms, arrhythmia history, medication, and renal function.

## 3. Management of interference
| Strategy | Detail |
|---|---|
| Reduce EMI | Use bipolar diathermy or ultrasonic (Harmonic) scalpel; short bursts (under 5 seconds); lowest effective energy; position the return pad so the current path is away from the generator and leads (for abdominal surgery, on the thigh or buttock); keep the cables away from the device |
| Monitoring | Pulse oximetry plethysmography or arterial line to confirm mechanical rhythm (ECG is distorted by diathermy); set ECG pacing spike detection on; keep external pacing and defibrillation pads in position; ensure that a defibrillator is immediately available |
| Pacemaker | If not pacing-dependent and surgery is below the umbilicus, no change is needed. For above-umbilical monopolar diathermy in a pacing-dependent patient, use a magnet (asynchronous pacing in most pacemakers, though not all; confirm in advance) or reprogram to an asynchronous mode (VOO/DOO) |
| ICD | A magnet suspends tachyarrhythmia therapies (does not affect bradycardia pacing). Alternatively, the device clinic programs tachy therapies off. Pads on and an external defibrillator are mandatory while therapies are suspended. Some devices have no magnet response |
| CRT | A magnet does not turn off biventricular pacing; check that there is high-percentage biventricular pacing preoperatively; AF or ventricular ectopy can reduce capture, and rate-adaptive pacing may increase heart rate in response to minute ventilation sensors (disable if needed) |
| Rate-responsive sensors | Minute ventilation sensors can be misled by ventilation or monitor signals; consider disabling |

## 4. If an arrhythmia occurs while the ICD is disabled
Treat as normal: defibrillate or cardiovert using pads, with anterior-posterior position, and keeping them at least 8 to 10 cm from the generator.

## 5. Postoperative management
- Re-enable ICD therapies before the patient leaves a monitored environment (never leave therapies disabled in the ward or at home).
- Re-interrogate if there was monopolar diathermy near the device, cardioversion, defibrillation, CPR, or if the device was reprogrammed; pacemakers should be checked within 1 month in other situations according to local policy.
- Monitor the ECG continuously until the device is checked.

## 6. Management of the underlying cardiomyopathy
Treat as HFrEF (see R10 and R11), continue guideline-directed medications, and use invasive monitoring.

## 7. Documentation and communication
Record the pre- and postoperative device status, the programming changes, the equipment used and the person responsible for restoring therapies; inform the patient.

> **Examiner lens:** never leave an ICD with therapies disabled outside a monitored environment.

items.title: Explain reperfusion in STEMI and list absolute and relative contraindications to fibrinolysis.
items.sub: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.eyebrow: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.q: Explain reperfusion in STEMI and list absolute and relative contraindications to fibrinolysis.
items.a:
- Primary PCI preferred: first medical contact to device within 90 minutes (60 if at a PCI centre).
- Fibrinolysis if PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes: within 30 minutes of arrival; give within 12 hours of onset.
- Rescue PCI if less than 50% ST resolution at 60 to 90 minutes; routine angiography 2 to 24 hours after successful lysis.
- Absolute contraindications: previous intracranial haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke within 6 months (some say 3), CNS neoplasm or AVM, major trauma, surgery or head injury within 3 weeks, GI bleeding within a month, known bleeding disorder, aortic dissection, non-compressible punctures.
- Relative: severe uncontrolled hypertension (above 180/110), TIA within 6 months, anticoagulation, pregnancy, traumatic CPR, peptic ulcer.
- Agents: tenecteplase, alteplase, reteplase.

> **Closing point:** Recent surgery usually rules out lysis, so favour PCI after surgery.

items.title: Define cardiogenic shock and describe the SCAI stages.
items.sub: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.eyebrow: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.q: Define cardiogenic shock and describe the SCAI stages.
items.a:
- Definition: sustained hypotension (SBP below 90 mmHg for 30 minutes or need for support) with signs of hypoperfusion (lactate above 2, oliguria, cool peripheries, altered mentation) and cardiac index below 2.2 L/min/m2 with raised filling pressures.
- Causes: acute MI (most common), mechanical complications, acute valve failure, myocarditis, decompensated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, tamponade, PE.
- SCAI stages: A at risk, B beginning (hypotension without hypoperfusion), C classic (hypoperfusion needing intervention), D deteriorating (not responding), E extremis (arrest, CPR, ECMO).
- Assessment: lactate, echo, arterial line, PAC for complex cases.
- Mortality about 40 to 50%.

> **Closing point:** Lactate and the response to initial therapy define the stage and the trajectory.

items.title: List the anaesthetic do's and don'ts in HCM with outflow obstruction.
items.sub: 6. Cardiomyopathy
items.eyebrow: 6. Cardiomyopathy
items.q: List the anaesthetic do's and don'ts in HCM with outflow obstruction.
items.a:
- Mechanism: SAM of the mitral valve in a small hyperdynamic LV; obstruction rises with contractility, falls with LV volume and afterload.
- Do: keep preload (fluids, avoid fasting), slow heart rate (esmolol, beta-blocker, volatile), maintain sinus rhythm (cardiovert AF early), keep SVR with phenylephrine or vasopressin.
- Do not: use inotropes, ephedrine, adrenaline, vasodilators (GTN, high-dose volatile), or tolerate hypovolaemia.
- Neuraxial: a slowly titrated epidural may be acceptable; a single-shot spinal is risky.
- Check the ICD, risk of sudden death.
- TOE: SAM, LVOT gradient, MR.

> **Closing point:** Full, slow and tight (preload, rate, afterload).

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
**Source check:** the linked pages were identified by title match; PubMed abstracts could not be opened in this session, so every figure below is from memory and should be checked against the paper before you quote it. Links marked DOI are from memory.

## 8.1 Perioperative risk and cardiac protection (Topic 1)

| Trial | Design | Key result | Exam message | Source check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [POISE](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18479744/) (Lancet 2008) | RCT, 8,351 patients, non-cardiac surgery; metoprolol CR 100 mg pre-op then 200 mg daily vs placebo | Fewer MIs (3.6 vs 5.1%) and lower composite of cardiac death, MI, arrest (5.8 vs 6.9%), but more deaths (3.1 vs 2.3%), stroke (1.0 vs 0.5%) and hypotension | Do not start high-dose beta-blocker on the day of surgery; continue chronic therapy | From memory |
| [POISE-2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24679062/) (NEJM 2014) | 2x2 factorial RCT, about 10,000 patients; aspirin vs placebo, clonidine vs placebo | Aspirin: no reduction in death or MI (about 7% both arms), more major bleeding. Clonidine: no benefit, more hypotension and non-fatal cardiac arrest | Do not start aspirin or clonidine for perioperative protection; continue aspirin in stented patients | From memory |
| [POISE-3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36053523/) (NEJM 2022) | 2x2 factorial RCT, about 9,500 patients; tranexamic acid vs placebo, plus hypotension-avoidance vs hypertension-avoidance strategy | TXA reduced composite bleeding (about 9 vs 12%) but non-inferiority for the composite vascular safety outcome was not established. The BP-strategy arm was reported separately | TXA reduces bleeding in major surgery; BP management has no simple trial-proven target | From memory; BP-strategy paper not located |
| [CARP](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15625331/) (NEJM 2004) | RCT, 510 patients with stable CAD before vascular surgery; revascularisation vs none | No difference in long-term mortality (about 22 vs 23%) or perioperative MI | No prophylactic revascularisation in stable CAD | From memory |
| [VISION troponin cohort](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28444280/) (JAMA 2017) | Prospective cohort, about 21,800 patients; peak postoperative hs-troponin T | 30-day mortality rises stepwise with peak troponin (about 4% at 20 to under 65 ng/L, about 9% at 65 to under 1,000 ng/L) | Defines MINS; justifies routine troponin surveillance in at-risk patients | From memory |
| [MANAGE report](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31629536/) (Lancet 2018) | RCT, about 1,750 patients with MINS; dabigatran 110 mg twice daily vs placebo | Fewer major vascular complications (about 11 vs 15%) without an increase in major bleeding | Treatment option for MINS; evidence limited by early stopping | From memory; confirm the original paper |
| [STOP-or-NOT](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39212270/) (JAMA 2024) | RCT, about 2,200 patients; continue vs stop ACEi/ARB 48 h before major surgery | No significant difference in the composite of death and major complications; more intraoperative hypotension with continuation | Either approach acceptable; withholding is reasonable in hypertensive patients | From memory |
| [METS](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30070222/) (Lancet 2018) | Prospective cohort, about 1,400 patients before major surgery | Subjective functional capacity did a poor job of predicting events; DASI and NT-proBNP predicted death or MI | Use DASI and BNP rather than clinical impression | From memory |
| [RCRI (Lee)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10477528/) (Circulation 1999) | Derivation and validation cohort | Six predictors; risk of major cardiac complication climbs with each | The standard bedside risk index | From memory |

## 8.2 Acute MI, cardiogenic shock and supportive care (Topic 2)

| Trial | Design | Key result | Exam message | Source check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [SHOCK](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10460813/) (NEJM 1999) | RCT, 302 patients with MI shock; early revascularisation vs initial medical stabilisation | 30-day mortality 46.7 vs 56.0% (not significant); 6-month mortality 50.3 vs 63.1% | Emergency revascularisation is the key treatment | From memory |
| [IABP-SHOCK II](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22920912/) (NEJM 2012) | RCT, 600 patients; IABP vs none | 30-day mortality 39.7 vs 41.3% | No routine IABP in MI shock | From memory |
| [CULPRIT-SHOCK](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29083953/) (NEJM 2017) | RCT, about 700 patients with multivessel disease; culprit-only PCI vs immediate multivessel PCI | Death or renal replacement at 30 days lower with culprit-only (45.9 vs 55.4%) | Treat the culprit vessel only in shock | From memory |
| [DanGer Shock](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38587239/) (NEJM 2024) | RCT, 360 STEMI-shock patients; Impella CP plus standard care vs standard care | 180-day mortality 45.8 vs 58.5%; more bleeding, limb ischaemia and renal replacement | Impella helps in selected STEMI shock (no coma, LV-predominant) | From memory |
| [ECLS-SHOCK](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307227) (NEJM 2023, DOI from memory) | RCT, 420 patients; early VA-ECMO vs standard care | 30-day mortality 47.8 vs 49.0%; more bleeding and vascular complications | VA-ECMO does not routinely improve survival in MI shock | From memory |
| [SOAP II](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20200382/) (NEJM 2010) | RCT, 1,679 patients with shock; dopamine vs noradrenaline | No overall mortality difference; more arrhythmias with dopamine; higher mortality in the cardiogenic shock subgroup with dopamine | Noradrenaline first line | From memory |
| [DETO2X-AMI](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28844200/) (NEJM 2017) | RCT, about 6,600 normoxic patients with suspected MI; oxygen vs room air | One-year mortality about 5% in both arms | No oxygen if SpO2 is 90% or more | From memory |
| [MINT](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37952133/) (NEJM 2023) | RCT, about 3,500 patients with MI and anaemia; restrictive vs liberal transfusion | Death or recurrent MI at 30 days: 16.9% restrictive vs 14.5% liberal (not significant, favours liberal) | Do not be aggressive about restrictive thresholds in acute MI | From memory |

## 8.3 Heart failure and pulmonary oedema (Topics 3 and 5)

| Trial | Design | Key result | Exam message | Source check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [PARADIGM-HF](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25176015/) (NEJM 2014) | RCT, about 8,400 HFrEF patients; sacubitril-valsartan vs enalapril | CV death or HF hospitalisation 21.8 vs 26.5% | ARNI is first-line in HFrEF | From memory |
| [DAPA-HF](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31535829/) (NEJM 2019) | RCT, about 4,700 HFrEF patients; dapagliflozin vs placebo | Worsening HF or CV death 16.3 vs 21.2%, benefit with or without diabetes | SGLT2 inhibitors for HFrEF; hold before surgery | From memory |
| [EMPEROR-Reduced](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32865377/) (NEJM 2020) | RCT, about 3,700 HFrEF patients; empagliflozin vs placebo | CV death or HF hospitalisation 19.4 vs 24.7% | Confirms SGLT2 inhibitor benefit | From memory |
| [DOSE](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21366472/) (NEJM 2011) | RCT, 308 patients with acute decompensated HF; bolus vs infusion and low vs high furosemide dose | No significant difference in symptom score; high dose gave more decongestion and more transient creatinine rise | Dose and mode of loop diuretic matter less than giving enough | From memory |
| [ESCAPE](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.294.13.1625) (JAMA 2005, DOI from memory) | RCT, about 430 patients with advanced HF; PAC-guided vs clinically guided therapy | No difference in days alive and out of hospital; more adverse events with PAC | No routine PAC in acute HF | From memory |
| [3CPO](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18987377/) (NEJM 2008) | RCT, about 1,070 patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; CPAP or NIV vs standard oxygen | 7-day mortality about 9.5 vs 9.8% (not significant); faster relief of dyspnoea and acidosis | NIV or CPAP helps symptoms; mortality benefit unproven | From memory |

## 8.4 Valves, anticoagulation and cardiomyopathy (Topics 4 and 6)

| Trial | Design | Key result | Exam message | Source check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [PARTNER 3](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1814052) (NEJM 2019, DOI from memory) | RCT, about 1,000 low-risk AS patients; TAVI (SAPIEN 3) vs surgery | Death, stroke or rehospitalisation at 1 year 8.5 vs 15.1% | TAVI is an option in low-risk AS | From memory |
| [COAPT](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30280640/) (NEJM 2018) | RCT, 614 HF patients with secondary MR; MitraClip plus medical therapy vs medical therapy | HF hospitalisation 35.8 vs 67.9 per 100 patient-years; 24-month mortality 29.1 vs 46.1% | Edge-to-edge repair in carefully selected secondary MR | From memory |
| [BRIDGE](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1501035) (NEJM 2015, DOI from memory) | RCT, about 1,900 AF patients on warfarin; LMWH bridging vs placebo | Thromboembolism 0.4 vs 0.3% (non-inferior without bridging); major bleeding 1.3 vs 3.2% | No bridging for most AF patients; mechanical valves were excluded | From memory |
| [INVICTUS](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36449436/) (NEJM 2022) | RCT, about 4,500 AF patients with rheumatic heart disease; rivaroxaban vs VKA | Higher rate of the composite outcome and death with rivaroxaban | VKA remains standard in rheumatic AF and moderate to severe MS | From memory |
| [EXPLORER-HCM](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(20)31792-X) (Lancet 2020, DOI from memory) | RCT, 251 symptomatic obstructive HCM patients; mavacamten vs placebo | Primary functional composite met by 37 vs 17% | Myosin inhibitor lowers LVOT gradient and improves function | From memory |

items.title: List the haemodynamic goals in aortic stenosis and the reasoning.
items.sub: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.eyebrow: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.q: List the haemodynamic goals in aortic stenosis and the reasoning.
items.a:
- Rate 60 to 80: allows ejection time and diastolic coronary filling.
- Rhythm: sinus, since the stiff LV needs atrial kick.
- Preload: maintain or slightly increase.
- Afterload: maintain SVR and perfusion pressure (hypotension causes ischaemia in the hypertrophied LV); vasopressor ready.
- Contractility: maintain; avoid depressant doses.
- Avoid: tachycardia, hypotension, vasodilation, neuraxial single-shot block, loss of sinus rhythm.
- Treat AF early with cardioversion; CPR is ineffective across a fixed obstruction.

> **Closing point:** The fixed obstruction means that cardiac output cannot rise, so protect coronary perfusion pressure.

items.title: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.los: IT_PO 1.4 (valvular heart disease component); SS_CS 1.4 (valve pathology component)
items.body:
## 4.1 General principles

- Stenotic lesions are **fixed-output** states and are poorly tolerated by vasodilation, tachycardia and hypovolaemia. Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (AS) and mitral stenosis (MS) carry the highest perioperative risk.
- Regurgitant lesions are volume-loaded and tolerate vasodilation, with moderate tachycardia, better than stenotic lesions.
- Acute valve failure (acute MR, AR) is far worse than chronic disease because the ventricle has not adapted.
- Preoperative assessment aims to define severity, symptoms, ventricular function, pulmonary pressures, rhythm, and anticoagulation.
- Elective non-cardiac surgery should be deferred for severe symptomatic stenosis until the valve is treated (surgical or transcatheter) unless the surgery is urgent.
- Endocarditis prophylaxis (AHA 2021 / Australian Therapeutic Guidelines): indicated only for dental procedures with gingival manipulation in the highest-risk group: prosthetic valve or material, previous endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic congenital disease, repaired congenital disease with prosthetic material within 6 months, and cardiac transplant valvulopathy. Not routinely required for GI or GU procedures.

## 4.2 Overview of severity and haemodynamics

| Lesion | Severe criteria (echo) | Ventricular response | Core haemodynamic goals |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aortic stenosis | AV area below 1.0 cm2 (indexed below 0.6), mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, peak velocity 4 m/s or more, dimensionless index below 0.25. Low-flow low-gradient forms exist | Concentric LVH, diastolic dysfunction, high LVEDP, subendocardial ischaemia | Preload full, rate 60 to 80 (sinus rhythm vital), afterload and SVR maintained, contractility preserved |
| Aortic regurgitation | Regurgitant volume 60 mL or more, fraction 50% or more, EROA 0.3 cm2 or more, vena contracta above 0.6 cm, pressure half-time below 200 ms, holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta | Eccentric dilatation (chronic); wide pulse pressure | Preload full, rate high-normal (80 to 100: shortens diastole), afterload low, contractility maintained |
| Mitral stenosis | MV area 1.5 cm2 or less (progressive MS 1.5 to 2 / severe below 1.5), mean gradient above 10 mmHg at HR 60 to 80, pressure half-time 150 ms or more | LA dilatation, AF, pulmonary hypertension, RV failure; normal LV | Preload adequate not excessive, rate slow (60 to 80, long diastole), sinus rhythm, keep SVR, avoid rises in PVR |
| Mitral regurgitation | EROA 0.4 cm2 or more, regurgitant volume 60 mL or more, vena contracta 0.7 cm or more, systolic flow reversal in pulmonary veins | LV dilatation, normal or low-normal EF 'flatters' LV (EF below 60% already indicates dysfunction) | Preload full, rate normal-to-high (80 to 100), afterload low, avoid raised SVR, support RV |
| Tricuspid | Rare in isolation | RV and RA overload | Maintain preload, avoid raised PVR |

> **Figure (diagram not reproduced):** valve lesions by heart rate and afterload goal. Rate and afterload goals split valve lesions into two groups; preload is kept full in all of them.

## 4.3 Aortic stenosis (most examinable)

**Aetiology:** age-related calcific degeneration (most common), bicuspid valve (younger patients), rheumatic. **Natural history:** long asymptomatic phase with slow progression (peak velocity rises about 0.3 m/s, mean gradient 7 mmHg per year, valve area falls about 0.1 cm2 per year); after the onset of symptoms, mean survival falls steeply: **angina about 5 years, syncope about 3 years, heart failure about 1 to 2 years**; high risk of sudden death once symptomatic.

**Echocardiographic features of haemodynamically significant AS:**

| Feature | Finding |
|---|---|
| Valve morphology | Thickened, calcified leaflets with restricted opening; bicuspid appearance in PLAX or SAX (TOE short axis at 30 to 60 degrees) |
| Peak velocity (CW Doppler through the valve) | 4.0 m/s or more (severe); 3.0 to 3.9 moderate |
| Mean gradient | 40 mmHg or more (severe) |
| Valve area (continuity equation) | AVA = (LVOT area x LVOT VTI) / AV VTI; below 1.0 cm2 severe |
| Dimensionless index (DVI) | LVOT VTI / AV VTI below 0.25 |
| LV | Concentric LVH, preserved or reduced EF, diastolic dysfunction (E/e' raised) |
| Other | Post-stenotic aortic root dilation, MR, LA enlargement, pulmonary hypertension (late) |
| Low-flow low-gradient AS | AVA below 1.0 cm2 with mean gradient below 40, EF below 50% or stroke volume index below 35 mL/m2 (paradoxical). Use dobutamine stress echo or CT calcium score (above 1,300 AU women, above 2,000 AU men) |

**Pathophysiology:** fixed LV outflow obstruction leads to concentric hypertrophy, raised LVEDP, increased wall tension and O2 demand, and reduced coronary flow reserve from elevated LVEDP and low DBP (subendocardial ischaemia in the absence of coronary disease). Loss of atrial kick (AF, junctional rhythm) causes sudden decompensation. Stroke volume cannot rise, so cardiac output depends on heart rate and rhythm.

**Anaesthetic management of severe AS:**

- Avoid the three killers: **hypotension, tachycardia, and loss of sinus rhythm**. Aim for HR 60 to 80, SR, MAP at or above baseline (65 to 70 minimum), euvolaemia to slightly full.
- Vasopressor first (phenylephrine, metaraminol, noradrenaline) at induction and during neuraxial block; avoid pure vasodilators. Pre-emptive vasopressor infusion.
- Defibrillator pads on; treat AF or SVT with early synchronised cardioversion.
- GA with controlled induction and slow titration; avoid spinal single-shot block (rapid sympathectomy); slow epidural or CSE and low-dose spinal with infusion of vasopressors have been used in selected cases.
- Invasive arterial line before induction; consider TOE for major surgery.
- Postoperative HDU.
- If severe symptomatic AS requires urgent non-cardiac surgery, balloon aortic valvuloplasty or TAVI may be considered as a bridge (see trials).

**Management of the valve:** SAVR (low surgical risk, age below 65 to 70) or TAVI (PARTNER 1, 3; SURTAVI; Evolut Low Risk) for symptomatic severe AS; mechanical vs bioprosthetic valve choice influences anticoagulation.

## 4.4 Aortic regurgitation

**Aetiology:** valve disease (bicuspid, rheumatic, endocarditis) or root dilatation (Marfan, hypertension, ankylosing spondylitis, aortic dissection).

**Pathophysiology:** volume overload, eccentric hypertrophy, large stroke volume with wide pulse pressure (peripheral signs: collapsing pulse, de Musset, Quincke), low DBP and reduced coronary perfusion. Acute AR (endocarditis, dissection): LV cannot dilate, so LVEDP rises, premature MV closure, pulmonary oedema and shock.

**Anaesthetic goals:** keep HR **80 to 100** (shortens diastole, reducing regurgitant time), avoid bradycardia (increases regurgitant volume per beat), maintain preload, **reduce SVR** (vasodilators help), maintain contractility. Avoid IABP (contraindicated).

## 4.5 Mitral stenosis

**Aetiology:** rheumatic heart disease (dominant in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Maori and Pacific communities in Australasia), calcific degeneration, congenital.

**Pathophysiology:** obstruction between LA and LV raises LA pressure, then pulmonary venous and arterial pressure, causing pulmonary congestion, pulmonary hypertension and RV failure. The LV is underfilled with preserved EF. **Heart rate dictates filling time:** tachycardia shortens diastole, raising the gradient (gradient depends on flow and diastolic time squared) and LA pressure, causing APO. AF is common (loss of atrial kick, thromboembolism, stroke).

**Perioperative management (including laparoscopic surgery):**

| Issue | Approach |
|---|---|
| Severity | Echo (mean gradient, MVA, PASP), symptoms (dyspnoea, orthopnoea, haemoptysis, embolism). Severe symptomatic MS should be treated (balloon valvotomy or surgery) before elective surgery |
| Rate and rhythm | Continue beta-blocker or diltiazem/digoxin for rate control; avoid premedication that causes anxiety and tachycardia. AF with rapid ventricular response: cardiovert if unstable; beta-blocker or amiodarone; avoid pure inotropes |
| Anticoagulation | AF with MS, or LA thrombus: warfarin (not DOACs in moderate-to-severe rheumatic MS: INVICTUS trial favoured VKA). Bridging as per CHEST 2022 |
| Preload | Maintain; avoid fluid overload (small increments) |
| PVR | Avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, nitrous oxide, lung hyperinflation; the RV must not fail |
| SVR | Maintain; avoid vasodilatation (neuraxial block with caution) |
| Pneumoperitoneum | Raised intrathoracic pressure, reduced venous return, CO2 absorption increasing PVR, steep head-down raises LA pressure; use low insufflation pressure (10 to 12 mmHg) and gentle positioning. This patient may be better off with open or regional/field technique depending on severity |
| Monitoring | Arterial line, large-bore access, CVP or PAC are of limited value (PCWP overestimates LVEDP in MS), TOE |
| Drugs | Avoid ketamine and pancuronium (tachycardia); use remifentanil or fentanyl for the pressor response; sugammadex preferred to neostigmine/atropine (reduces tachycardia) |
| Postoperative | HDU; analgesia; early extubation with careful reversal |

## 4.6 Mitral regurgitation

**Primary (degenerative: prolapse, flail, endocarditis, rheumatic) vs secondary (functional: LV dilatation, ischaemic).** Severity depends on the loading conditions, so measure the regurgitation under anaesthesia. Chronic severe MR leads to LA dilatation (large compliance) and AF, then pulmonary hypertension.

**Assessment:** define the mechanism (Carpentier type I normal motion with annular dilation or perforation, II prolapse or flail, IIIa restricted in diastole, IIIb restricted in systole), severity by an integrated approach (EROA, regurgitant volume, vena contracta, pulmonary vein flow reversal), and the consequences: LV size and function, LA size, rhythm (AF), PASP and RV function. In chronic severe MR the LV ejects into a low-pressure LA, which **flatters the ejection fraction**: an EF of 60% or less, or an end-systolic diameter of 40 mm or more, already signals LV dysfunction. BNP and exercise tolerance help detect decompensation.

**Haemodynamic goals:**

| Variable | Goal | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Preload | Maintain; avoid both hypovolaemia and overload | Regurgitant volume depends on LA and LV filling |
| Heart rate | Normal to slightly fast (80 to 100) | Shorter diastole and smaller LV reduce the regurgitant orifice and volume |
| Afterload | Keep SVR low to normal | Vasoconstriction increases regurgitant fraction; vasodilators promote forward flow |
| Contractility | Maintain or support | A failing LV loses the low-impedance escape into the LA |
| Rhythm | Rate-control AF; keep sinus rhythm where possible | Loss of atrial contribution reduces filling |
| Pulmonary vascular resistance | Keep low | Pulmonary hypertension from chronic LA hypertension threatens RV function |

**Pulmonary hypertension and RV protection in MR:** avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia, pain and light anaesthesia, avoid nitrous oxide and high airway pressures, maintain PaCO2 35 to 40 mmHg and pH above 7.35, and keep PEEP modest. Use inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (nitric oxide or epoprostenol) or milrinone when pressures are high, support the RV with dobutamine or milrinone, and maintain systemic pressure above pulmonary artery pressure with noradrenaline or vasopressin to preserve RV coronary perfusion.

**Technique and monitoring:**

- Either general anaesthesia (opioid-based balanced technique; avoid agents that cause bradycardia or marked myocardial depression) or a carefully titrated neuraxial or regional technique are acceptable; neuraxial block reduces afterload and is usually well tolerated in MR, unlike in stenotic lesions.
- Arterial line, large-bore access and ECG with ST analysis; TOE for major surgery and for any instability, because intraoperative loading conditions change the degree of regurgitation (and ischaemic or functional MR is dynamic).
- Treat intraoperative hypotension with agents that avoid raising SVR excessively (small doses of noradrenaline or vasopressin plus inotrope if the LV is failing); avoid bradycardia.
- Acute severe MR (papillary muscle rupture, endocarditis, chordal rupture) presents with pulmonary oedema and shock and needs afterload reduction (nitroprusside), inotropes, IABP support and urgent surgery.

## 4.7 Prosthetic valves and anticoagulation

| Type | Antithrombotic therapy | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanical AVR (bileaflet, no risk factors) | Warfarin INR 2.5 (range 2.0 to 3.0) | Lifelong |
| Mechanical AVR with risk factors (AF, previous thromboembolism, LV dysfunction, hypercoagulable) or older-generation valve | INR 3.0 (2.5 to 3.5) | |
| Mechanical MVR | INR 3.0 (2.5 to 3.5) | Higher thrombotic risk than AVR |
| Bioprosthetic | Aspirin or warfarin 3 to 6 months after surgery | |
| TAVI | Aspirin; short DAPT or DOAC only if indicated | |
| DOAC | Contraindicated with mechanical valves (RE-ALIGN, dabigatran) | |

**Perioperative anticoagulation for a warfarinised patient with a mechanical valve:** stop warfarin 5 days before surgery (INR 1.5 or below for most surgery; neuraxial at INR below 1.4); **bridging with therapeutic LMWH or UFH is indicated for mechanical mitral valve, caged-ball or tilting disc valve, mechanical valve with a stroke or TIA in the last 6 months, or AF with multiple risk factors**; bridging is not needed for bileaflet aortic valve without risk factors (BRIDGE trial in AF showed no benefit and more bleeding). Start heparin when INR falls below 2.0 (about day 2 to 3), last therapeutic LMWH dose 24 h before surgery (half dose if the surgery is major or neuraxial planned), restart the day after surgery when haemostasis is secure (48 to 72 h for high-bleeding-risk surgery).

**Reversal in an emergency:** vitamin K 1 to 2 mg IV is acceptable (avoid high dose, which makes re-warfarinisation difficult); prothrombin complex concentrate (25 to 50 units/kg) with vitamin K for life-threatening bleeding; FFP less preferred.

**Mechanical heart valves in pregnancy:**

- Highest-risk anticoagulation decision. Warfarin is the most effective for maternal valve protection but is teratogenic (embryopathy: weeks 6 to 12 and fetal bleeding), LMWH or UFH does not cross the placenta but has higher valve thrombosis risk (dose by anti-Xa peak 0.8 to 1.2 U/mL 4 to 6 h post dose, trough above 0.6).
- Options per ESC/ACC: warfarin throughout if dose 5 mg/day or less; LMWH or UFH in the first trimester (weeks 6 to 12) then warfarin from week 13 to week 36; at 36 weeks switch to LMWH or IV UFH; **stop LMWH 24 h before planned delivery** (or IV UFH 4 to 6 h before) for neuraxial block, or switch to IV UFH; recommence the heparin 6 to 12 h after delivery (neuraxial catheter removal at 12 h post prophylactic dose, 24 h after therapeutic); restart warfarin 24 to 48 h and bridge until INR therapeutic; warfarin and breastfeeding is compatible.
- Delivery planning with a multidisciplinary team (cardiology, obstetrics, anaesthesia, haematology) and avoid delivery on warfarin (fetal intracranial haemorrhage risk, preference for caesarean if on warfarin).

## 4.8 Assessment of valve disease (SS_CS 1.4)

| Modality | Information |
|---|---|
| Clinical | Murmur (AS: ejection systolic radiating to carotids; MR: pansystolic to axilla; MS: mid-diastolic rumble with opening snap; AR: early diastolic decrescendo), pulse character, S3/S4, JVP, signs of RV failure |
| ECG | LVH, AF, left atrial enlargement (P mitrale), conduction disease |
| Echo | Valve morphology and mobility, severity (above), chamber size, EF, PASP, RV function, vegetations; TOE for detail and intraoperative use |
| CMR / CT | Quantification of regurgitation; CT for TAVI planning and calcium scoring |
| Catheterisation | Haemodynamics when echo is discordant; coronary angiography before valve surgery |

**Intraoperative TOE views for valves:** ME 4-chamber, ME 2-chamber, ME LAX (MV), ME AV SAX (AV morphology), ME AV LAX (AR jet width, root), TG LAX and deep TG (CW Doppler gradient), colour Doppler jets. Use the Carpentier classification (Type I normal leaflet motion, II prolapse, III restricted: IIIa diastolic, IIIb systolic) for MR mechanism.

items.title: Give the immediate management of cardiogenic acute pulmonary oedema.
items.sub: 5. Acute pulmonary oedema
items.eyebrow: 5. Acute pulmonary oedema
items.q: Give the immediate management of cardiogenic acute pulmonary oedema.
items.a:
- Sit upright, oxygen to SpO2 94% or more, monitor and IV access.
- CPAP or NIV (3CPO: faster symptom relief; mortality not different).
- GTN (sublingual, then IV) if SBP is adequate; avoid if hypotensive, severe AS or RV infarct.
- IV loop diuretic (furosemide 20 to 40 mg or higher with renal dysfunction).
- Treat the cause: ACS, arrhythmia, hypertension, valve failure.
- Opioids no longer favoured (worse outcomes, respiratory depression).
- Intubate if exhaustion, acidosis or failure of NIV.

> **Closing point:** CPAP and nitrate treat the pressure; the diuretic is slower.

items.title: Compare clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor and cangrelor, including the stop time before surgery.
items.sub: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.eyebrow: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.q: Compare clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor and cangrelor, including the stop time before surgery.
items.a:
- Clopidogrel: oral prodrug, irreversible, CYP2C19 activation (variable response); stop 5 to 7 days.
- Prasugrel: oral prodrug, irreversible, more potent and consistent; stop 7 days; avoid with prior stroke, age 75 or over, or weight below 60 kg.
- Ticagrelor: oral, direct acting, reversible; stop 3 to 5 days; dyspnoea and bradycardia side effects.
- Cangrelor: IV, reversible, half-life 3 to 6 minutes; used as a bridge.
- Reversal: platelet transfusion works only after the active drug has cleared (ticagrelor and active clopidogrel metabolite inactivate transfused platelets).

> **Closing point:** Irreversible agents need platelet turnover (7 days); reversible agents wash out sooner.

items.title: Describe your choice of vasoactive drugs in cardiogenic shock.
items.sub: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.eyebrow: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.q: Describe your choice of vasoactive drugs in cardiogenic shock.
items.a:
- Target MAP of about 65 mmHg and restoration of perfusion (lactate, urine output).
- Noradrenaline first line (SOAP II: dopamine caused more arrhythmia and higher mortality in the cardiogenic subgroup).
- Add dobutamine (beta-1) for low output; risks are tachycardia, arrhythmia and ischaemia.
- Milrinone or enoximone: inodilators, not dependent on beta receptors; accumulate in renal failure; vasodilation.
- Levosimendan: calcium sensitiser, vasodilator; evidence limited.
- Adrenaline: effective but raises lactate and arrhythmia (CAPITAL DOREMI compared milrinone and dobutamine without a difference in outcome).
- Vasopressin as an adjunct to spare catecholamines and avoid raising PVR.
- Use the lowest dose for the shortest time; early mechanical support if drug doses escalate.

> **Closing point:** Support perfusion pressure first, then flow, and avoid adding myocardial oxygen demand.

items.title: 13. Echocardiographic assessment of LV function and filling
items.q: Describe how you assess LV systolic function, diastolic function and filling status with echo, and how the findings alter a fluid decision in theatre.
items.a:
## 1. Why echo
TTE or TOE provides a rapid, direct assessment of ventricular function, filling, valves, pericardium and volume status in the anaesthetic or ICU setting, and is recommended in unexplained haemodynamic instability (ASE/SCA and ANZCA guidance).

## 2. Systolic function
- **Qualitative:** visual estimate of LV function across views (mid-oesophageal four-chamber, two-chamber, long axis; transgastric mid short-axis), with the wall motion assessed in the 17-segment model (normal, hypokinetic, akinetic, dyskinetic). A new regional wall motion abnormality (RWMA) suggests ischaemia.
- **Quantitative:** biplane Simpson method (normal EF 52 to 72% in men and 54 to 74% in women), fractional area change from the transgastric mid short-axis view (normal 35 to 65%), fractional shortening, mitral annular systolic velocity (S'), and global longitudinal strain (normal about -18 to -22%, a sensitive marker of early dysfunction).
- **Stroke volume and cardiac output:** LVOT diameter and velocity time integral (VTI): SV = LVOT area x VTI; CO = SV x HR. A VTI below 18 to 20 cm suggests low stroke volume.
- **Pitfalls:** EF depends on loading conditions (it is overestimated in MR and vasodilation, underestimated in high afterload), is poor in the presence of RWMA or paced rhythm, and is unreliable in tachycardia.

## 3. Diastolic function
- Measurements: mitral inflow E and A velocities, E/A ratio, deceleration time, septal and lateral e' (tissue Doppler), average E/e', left atrial volume index, and TR velocity.
- The four screening criteria (ASE/EACVI 2016): septal e' below 7 or lateral e' below 10 cm/s; average E/e' above 14; LAVI above 34 mL/m2; TR velocity above 2.8 m/s. If more than half are positive, diastolic dysfunction is present; if fewer than half, it is normal; if half, it is indeterminate.
- Grades: I (impaired relaxation, E/A below 0.8, normal filling pressure), II (pseudonormal, E/A 0.8 to 2, E/e' 10 to 14, raised filling pressure), III (restrictive, E/A above 2, DT below 160 ms, high filling pressure).
- Limitations: AF (no A wave), significant MR, mitral stenosis, annular calcification, prosthetic valve, tachycardia, and a hyperdynamic LV.

## 4. Filling status and fluid responsiveness
| Parameter | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| LV end-diastolic area (TG SAX) | Small with kissing papillary muscles suggests hypovolaemia (but also vasoplegia or hyperdynamic state) |
| IVC (subcostal; TTE) | Diameter 2.1 cm or less with more than 50% inspiratory collapse suggests RAP about 3 mmHg; above 2.1 cm with less than 50% collapse suggests RAP about 15 mmHg. Unreliable in ventilated patients |
| SVC collapsibility (TOE) | Over 36% collapsibility predicts fluid responsiveness in ventilated patients |
| LVOT VTI variation | A rise of 10 to 15% after a passive leg raise or a 250 mL bolus predicts responsiveness |
| Pulse pressure or stroke volume variation | Above 12 to 13% predicts responsiveness if the patient is in sinus rhythm, ventilated with tidal volumes of 8 mL/kg or more and a closed chest |
| E/e' | Raised E/e' (above 14) suggests elevated LA pressure and a risk of pulmonary oedema with fluid |
| CVP and PAOP | Poor predictors of responsiveness, but high values indicate risk of congestion |

## 5. Applying to the decision to give fluid
- Is the patient hypoperfused or unstable? (Fluid is not indicated if the problem is not preload.)
- Is the patient likely to respond? (Dynamic tests above.)
- Is the patient likely to tolerate fluid? (No raised E/e', no significant RV failure or congestion, no severe valve lesion; lung ultrasound B-lines suggest limited tolerance.)
- If yes to all: give a 250 mL balanced crystalloid bolus and re-measure SV or VTI. If not: use a vasopressor, inotrope or both, and treat the cause.

## 6. Take-home points
Combine function, filling and responsiveness; fluid responsiveness does not equal fluid need, and a heart that responds may still be congested.

> **Examiner lens:** fluid responsiveness is not the same as fluid need; combine dynamic and static measures.

items.title: 5. Acute pulmonary oedema
items.body:
## 5.1 Pathophysiology

**Starling forces across the pulmonary capillary:** Jv = Kf x [(Pc - Pi) - sigma x (pi_c - pi_i)]. Oedema forms when capillary hydrostatic pressure rises, oncotic pressure falls, permeability rises (sigma falls, Kf rises), or lymphatic drainage is overwhelmed. Lymphatic flow can increase about tenfold before oedema forms, and the alveolar epithelium is the final barrier, so oedema appears in the interstitium (Kerley lines, peribronchial cuffing) before flooding alveoli.

| Category | Mechanism | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Cardiogenic (haemostatic) | Raised pulmonary venous pressure (PAOP above 18 mmHg) | LV failure (ischaemia, hypertensive crisis, cardiomyopathy), MS, acute MR or AR, arrhythmia, fluid overload, renal failure |
| Non-cardiogenic (permeability) | Capillary leak, normal PAOP (18 mmHg or less) | ARDS, sepsis, aspiration, trauma, TRALI, pancreatitis |
| Mixed or other | Reduced oncotic pressure, lymphatic obstruction, negative pressure | Negative pressure pulmonary oedema (laryngospasm, airway obstruction), neurogenic, re-expansion, high-altitude, opioid or salicylate toxicity, upper-airway obstruction, TACO |

**Physiological consequences:** reduced compliance (increased work of breathing), shunt and V/Q mismatch (hypoxaemia), and increased sympathetic drive (hypertension, tachycardia, high afterload creates a vicious circle). Positive pressure acts by reducing venous return (preload), lowering LV transmural pressure (afterload), recruiting alveoli, and reducing work of breathing.

**Perioperative triggers:** fluid overload or TACO, myocardial ischaemia, new arrhythmia (AF), hypertensive crisis (emergence), negative pressure pulmonary oedema (after extubation with laryngospasm or airway obstruction; occurs in young, fit patients, resolves in 24 to 48 h), aspiration, anaphylaxis, TRALI or transfusion-associated circulatory overload, neurogenic oedema (subarachnoid haemorrhage, head injury), sepsis or SIRS, drug reaction (protamine), PE, and pre-eclampsia.

## 5.2 Clinical features and diagnosis

- **Symptoms:** acute breathlessness, orthopnoea, agitation, cough with pink frothy sputum.
- **Signs:** tachypnoea, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension (or shock), S3 gallop, bilateral crackles and wheeze ('cardiac asthma'), raised JVP, hypoxaemia.
- **Investigations:** ABG (hypoxaemia, type 1 then type 2 failure with fatigue), ECG (ischaemia, arrhythmia), troponin, BNP/NT-proBNP (high negative predictive value; raised in cardiac but also in renal failure and PE), CXR (bat-wing perihilar shadowing, cardiomegaly, Kerley B lines, effusions; non-cardiogenic oedema shows peripheral patchy shadows and normal heart size), lung ultrasound (B lines: 3 or more per field bilaterally), bedside echo (LV function, valves, IVC, effusion, E/e').

**Differential diagnosis of perioperative pulmonary oedema and acute dyspnoea with frothy secretions:**

| Diagnosis | Clues | Key action |
|---|---|---|
| Negative pressure pulmonary oedema | After laryngospasm or airway obstruction; young and fit; rapid onset | Relieve obstruction; oxygen with CPAP or PEEP; resolves in 12 to 48 h |
| Cardiogenic (LV failure, ischaemia, arrhythmia, valve lesion) | Cardiac history, hypertension, ECG change, raised troponin or BNP | Vasodilator, diuretic, treat ischaemia or rhythm |
| Fluid overload or TACO | Large positive balance, raised JVP, hypertension, responds to diuresis | Stop fluids, diuretic |
| Aspiration (gastric contents or blood) | Witnessed regurgitation or airway soiling; wheeze; focal infiltrate | Suction, oxygen, supportive ventilation |
| Anaphylaxis | Hypotension, bronchospasm, rash, recent drug exposure | Adrenaline; fluid; stop trigger |
| TRALI | Within 6 h of transfusion, fever, hypotension, bilateral infiltrates, normal or low BNP | Supportive (no diuretics); report to the blood service |
| Pulmonary embolism | Sudden hypoxia, tachycardia, raised ETCO2 gradient, right heart strain | See PE guidance |
| Bronchospasm or asthma | Wheeze, prolonged expiration, high peak pressures | Bronchodilators |
| Pneumothorax | Unilateral signs, hypotension, high airway pressure | Decompress |

Management follows the cause: secure the airway and oxygenation, apply CPAP or PEEP, obtain an ECG, troponin, chest X-ray or lung ultrasound, and treat the specific diagnosis.

## 5.3 Initial management (IT_RT 1.2, SS_IC 1.45)

**Principles:** sit upright, high-flow oxygen, early positive pressure, vasodilator, diuretic (if volume-overloaded), and treat the precipitant. Use the mnemonic of immediate steps: **S** it up, **O** xygen/CPAP, **N** itrate, **D** iuretic, **I** nvestigate, **T** reat cause (and the opioid is no longer favoured).

| Step | Details | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Position and oxygen | Sit up with legs dependent; high-flow oxygen aiming SpO2 94 to 98% | |
| CPAP or NIV | CPAP 5 to 10 cmH2O or BiPAP (IPAP 10 to 15 / EPAP 5 to 8) reduces work of breathing, intubation rate and short-term mortality in some meta-analyses | 3CPO: NIV improved dyspnoea, heart rate, acidosis and hypercapnia faster but did not reduce 7-day mortality; CPAP and NIV are equivalent |
| Vasodilator | GTN spray 400 micrograms SL, then infusion 10 to 200 micrograms/min if SBP above 110 (preload and afterload reduction, coronary dilation); sodium nitroprusside for hypertensive crisis | GTN effective in hypertensive acute HF; high-dose isosorbide dinitrate bolus with low-dose furosemide (Cotter) reduced intubation |
| Loop diuretic | Furosemide 40 to 80 mg IV (venodilatation first, diuresis in 15 to 30 min). Lower doses in diuretic-naive patients (20 to 40 mg); higher doses in chronic users | DOSE |
| Opioid | Morphine is no longer recommended routinely (ADHERE: higher mechanical ventilation, ICU admission and mortality in observational data); small doses may help anxiety | |
| Treat precipitant | Ischaemia (reperfusion), arrhythmia (cardioversion), hypertension (vasodilator), valve emergencies (surgery), fluid overload (diuresis, dialysis), anaemia (transfuse) | |
| Intubation | Hypoxaemia and exhaustion despite NIV, GCS reduction, shock, inability to protect the airway. Induce cautiously: pre-oxygenate with CPAP, ketamine or etomidate, vasopressor ready; PEEP up to 10 to 15 cmH2O reduces venous return and afterload | |
| Inotropes and MCS | For hypotension, cold and wet profile (see Topic 3) | |

**Intraoperative pulmonary oedema:**

- Call for help; 100% oxygen; check airway, tube position, ventilation and circuit (rule out airway problem, tube obstruction, endobronchial migration).
- Stop IV fluids and anything causing fluid load; stop surgical irrigation; announce to the surgeon, consider abbreviating the operation.
- Increase PEEP (5 to 10 cmH2O), prolong expiratory time, ventilate to maintain SpO2; suction frothy secretions through the ETT.
- Diagnose the type: ECG and ST analysis, arterial blood gas, ETCO2 (PE), lung ultrasound, TOE (RWMA, valve, LV function), look for anaphylaxis (bronchospasm, flushing, hypotension), transfusion reaction, or negative pressure.
- Treat: vasodilator (GTN) if hypertensive, diuretic if overloaded, inotrope if low output, antiarrhythmic or cardioversion, treat ischaemia, adrenaline if anaphylaxis.
- Plan postoperative ICU/HDU, ventilation, and investigations (troponin, echo, BNP).

## 5.4 Special types

| Type | Notes |
|---|---|
| Negative pressure pulmonary oedema (Type I: acute obstruction; Type II: chronic obstruction relieved) | Forced inspiration against an obstructed airway generates very negative intrapleural pressure (up to -100 cmH2O), increasing venous return and transmural capillary pressure, with sympathetic surge and hypoxia injuring capillaries. Treatment: relieve obstruction, O2, CPAP or PEEP; usually resolves in 12 to 24 h; diuretics seldom needed |
| TACO vs TRALI | TACO: hypertension, raised JVP, raised BNP, responds to diuretic. TRALI: hypotension, fever, normal or low BNP, bilateral infiltrates within 6 h of transfusion, treat as ARDS (no diuretics), and report to the blood service. See Haemorrhage and Transfusion set |
| Re-expansion pulmonary oedema | After rapid drainage of a large pneumothorax or effusion: limit drainage to 1 to 1.5 L at once |
| Neurogenic pulmonary oedema | Sympathetic surge raising pulmonary venous pressure and capillary permeability; treat the neurological cause, supportive ventilation, alpha-blockade in some cases |
| Pre-eclampsia, peripartum cardiomyopathy | Obstetrics sets |

## 5.5 Cardiogenic versus non-cardiogenic oedema (SS_IC 1.45)

| Feature | Cardiogenic | Non-cardiogenic (ARDS) |
|---|---|---|
| History | Cardiac disease, ischaemia, volume overload | Sepsis, aspiration, trauma, transfusion |
| Heart size / vascular pedicle | Enlarged, wide pedicle | Normal heart, narrow pedicle |
| Distribution on CXR | Central perihilar, basal, effusions | Peripheral, patchy, air bronchograms |
| BNP | Raised (above 400 ng/L) | Mildly raised or normal |
| PAOP | Above 18 mmHg | 18 mmHg or less |
| Echo | Poor LV function, valve lesion | Normal LV |
| Oedema fluid protein : plasma protein | Below 0.5 | Above 0.7 |
| Response to diuretic and vasodilator | Prompt | Little |

items.title: 8. Cardiogenic shock: drug and device choices and what the trials say
items.q: A 60-year-old with anterior STEMI is in cardiogenic shock after PCI. Describe your haemodynamic and mechanical support strategy and the evidence behind it.
items.a:
## 1. Definition and assessment
- Cardiogenic shock is a state of low cardiac output with end-organ hypoperfusion despite adequate intravascular volume. Definition: SBP below 90 mmHg for 30 minutes (or vasopressors needed to maintain it), with evidence of hypoperfusion (lactate above 2 mmol/L, oliguria, cool and clammy skin, altered mentation) and a cardiac index below 2.2 L/min/m2 with elevated filling pressures (PAOP above 15).
- The SCAI classification (A to E) guides escalation: stage C (hypoperfusion needing intervention), D (deteriorating) and E (extremis, arrest).
- Mortality is 40 to 50% despite revascularisation. Anterior STEMI with shock is a high-risk category.
- Assess with: a 12-lead ECG, lactate, an arterial line, echo (LV function, RV function, mechanical complications, tamponade), and a PA catheter in complex shock, mixed shock or to guide escalation (it is associated with better outcomes in some registries, but not in randomised trials in general).

## 2. Immediate priorities
- Emergency revascularisation of the culprit artery, the only intervention proven to lower mortality (SHOCK trial: early revascularisation reduced 6 month mortality, with 132 survivors per 1000 treated at 1 year; absolute benefit of about 13% at 6 months).
- Haemodynamic support while this occurs.
- Treat the precipitants and complications (arrhythmia, mechanical complications, RV infarction, tamponade, bleeding).
- Support organs: ventilation if needed (cautious induction, see R10), renal replacement, glucose and temperature control.

## 3. Revascularisation strategy
- CULPRIT-SHOCK (706 patients with multivessel disease): treating only the culprit lesion at the index procedure had lower 30 day death or renal replacement than immediate multivessel PCI (45.9% vs 55.4%); staged PCI of non-culprit vessels if needed.
- Radial access, minimal contrast, and rapid door-to-balloon time.
- Immediate CABG for left main or severe multivessel disease not suitable for PCI.

## 4. Drug therapy
| Drug | Role and evidence |
|---|---|
| Noradrenaline | First line vasopressor; SOAP II (1679 patients) found more arrhythmia with dopamine, and in the cardiogenic shock subgroup higher 28 day mortality (RR 1.2) |
| Dobutamine | Beta-1 agonist for low cardiac output once the MAP is adequate; arrhythmogenic, raises myocardial oxygen demand |
| Milrinone | Inodilator, does not depend on beta receptors, but vasodilates and has a long half-life in renal impairment; CAPITAL DOREMI found no difference in outcomes between milrinone and dobutamine |
| Adrenaline | Effective but raises lactate and arrhythmia; in a randomised comparison of adrenaline with noradrenaline (OptimaCC) adrenaline caused more refractory shock |
| Vasopressin | An adjunct to spare catecholamines without raising PVR |
| Levosimendan | Calcium sensitiser; limited evidence |

Principles: lowest dose, shortest duration, because all increase myocardial oxygen consumption.

## 5. Mechanical circulatory support
| Device | Evidence and comment |
|---|---|
| IABP | IABP-SHOCK II (600 patients): no reduction in 30 day mortality (39.7% vs 41.3%) or at 12 months; downgraded in guidelines to class III in routine shock, though still used as a bridge for mechanical complications |
| Impella CP | DanGer Shock (360 patients with STEMI shock): lower mortality at 180 days (45.8% vs 58.5%), with more severe bleeding, limb ischaemia, and renal replacement. Applies to selected STEMI shock (LVEF below 45%, no hypoxic brain injury) |
| VA-ECMO | ECLS-SHOCK (420 patients): no mortality benefit at 30 days in unselected patients (47.8% vs 49.0%), with more bleeding and vascular complications. Used for refractory shock, arrest (ECPR), and biventricular or respiratory failure. LV venting may be needed (Impella, IABP, atrial septostomy) |
| ECMO plus Impella (ECPELLA) | Observational data suggest lower mortality; no randomised trial |

The decision is made by a multidisciplinary shock team, with early escalation (SCAI stage C to D) rather than late rescue.

## 6. Other support
- Fluids only if hypovolaemic or RV infarct.
- Ventilation: be cautious with intubation, which can cause collapse (see R10).
- Treat arrhythmia, acidosis, anaemia (a Hb of 80 to 100 g/L is the common threshold), and glucose.
- Early renal replacement and organ support in ICU.

## 7. Summary
Revascularise the culprit, support the pressure with noradrenaline, add an inotrope for low output, and consider selected mechanical support early as a bridge in a shock team model.

> **Examiner lens:** quote SCAI stage, revascularise first, and know that device trials are mixed.
