items.sub: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.eyebrow: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.q: How do you assess functional capacity and why does it matter?
items.a:
- Why: poor capacity predicts perioperative and long-term cardiac events.
- METs: 1 MET is basal; 4 METs is two flights of stairs or a brisk walk; above 10 is strenuous exercise.
- DASI: a 12-item questionnaire; score below 34 predicts higher events (METS study); better than subjective impression.
- Objective: CPET (anaerobic threshold below 11 mL/kg/min predicts risk), 6-minute walk.
- Use: poor capacity plus elevated-risk surgery prompts BNP, optimisation, or further testing only if it changes management.

> **Closing point:** Subjective assessment is unreliable; use a structured tool.

items.title: List the determinants of myocardial oxygen supply and demand and say how anaesthesia can disturb the balance.
items.sub: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.eyebrow: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.q: List the determinants of myocardial oxygen supply and demand and say how anaesthesia can disturb the balance.
items.a:
- Supply = coronary blood flow x arterial O2 content; coronary perfusion pressure = aortic diastolic pressure minus LVEDP (RV also in systole).
- Flow determinants: diastolic time (heart rate), perfusion pressure, vessel tone and stenosis, autoregulation, blood viscosity.
- Content determinants: haemoglobin, SaO2, PaO2.
- Demand: heart rate, wall tension (preload, afterload, LV size, Laplace), contractility.
- Anaesthetic threats: tachycardia, hypotension, anaemia, hypoxia, hypertension, pain, light anaesthesia, shivering.

> **Closing point:** Tachycardia hurts both sides at once, shortening diastole (supply) and raising demand.

items.title: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.priority: P1 CORE (3 parent LOs) + acute myocardial ischaemia crisis component at P2 HIGH
items.los: SS_CS 1.26; SS_IC 1.31; SS_CS 1.4 (myocardial ischaemia component); IT_RT 1.2 (acute myocardial ischaemia component)
items.body:
## 2.1 Recognition and diagnosis

**Clinical features:** central chest pain (often absent under GA or in diabetics, the elderly and after surgery), dyspnoea, sweating, nausea, arrhythmia, hypotension, new heart failure or cardiogenic shock. Perioperatively, suspect MI with unexplained hypotension, arrhythmia, pulmonary oedema, new ST change, desaturation or agitation.

**Fourth Universal Definition of MI:** a rise and/or fall of cardiac troponin with at least one value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit, together with at least one of: ischaemic symptoms; new ischaemic ECG changes; development of pathological Q waves; imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium or new regional wall motion abnormality; or coronary thrombus on angiography or autopsy.

**ECG criteria (acute ischaemia):**

| Finding | Criteria |
|---|---|
| STEMI | New ST elevation at the J point in 2 contiguous leads: at least 1 mm in all leads except V2 to V3, where it is at least 2 mm in men aged 40 or over (2.5 mm under 40), at least 1.5 mm in women |
| NSTEMI / unstable angina | ST depression (at least 0.5 mm in 2 contiguous leads), T wave inversion (at least 1 mm in leads with prominent R wave) or no change |
| Posterior MI | ST depression V1 to V3 with tall R waves; confirm with posterior leads V7 to V9 |
| Right ventricular MI | ST elevation in V4R, with inferior MI: avoid nitrates and diuretics, support with fluids |
| Equivalents | New LBBB (apply Sgarbossa criteria), de Winter T waves, Wellens' sign (critical LAD stenosis), hyperacute T waves, left main occlusion (ST elevation aVR with diffuse ST depression) |

| Territory | Leads | Artery |
|---|---|---|
| Anterior | V1 to V4 | LAD |
| Septal | V1 to V2 | LAD (septal perforators) |
| Lateral | I, aVL, V5 to V6 | LCx or diagonal |
| Inferior | II, III, aVF | RCA (80%), LCx |
| Posterior | ST depression V1 to V3 | RCA or LCx |
| RV | V4R | Proximal RCA |

**Troponin interpretation:** high-sensitivity troponin rises 3 to 4 h after injury, peaks at 24 to 48 h, and stays elevated 7 to 14 days. Use serial measurements (0 and 1 to 3 h algorithms). Non-MI causes of elevation include PE, sepsis, renal failure, myocarditis, arrhythmia, takotsubo, aortic dissection and cardiac contusion. CK-MB is largely obsolete.

## 2.2 Detection and investigation after surgery

- 12-lead ECG immediately and serially (compare with the preoperative ECG; absent baseline is a common exam trap).
- Serial hs-troponin; CK-MB only if troponin unavailable.
- Bedside echo (FoCUS/TTE): new RWMA, LV function, pericardial effusion, RV strain, valve lesion, mechanical complication.
- Chest X-ray, ABG, electrolytes (K, Mg), Hb, lactate, renal function, glucose, coagulation.
- Differential: PE, aortic dissection, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, pericarditis, oesophageal pathology, takotsubo, myocarditis, anaemia or hypovolaemia with demand ischaemia.
- Coronary angiography for STEMI, high-risk NSTEMI, or unexplained shock.

## 2.3 Initial medical management

Standard ACS approach (Australian Heart Foundation / CSANZ guideline; ESC 2023 ACS guideline), adapted to the perioperative bleeding risk. Never delay reperfusion for investigations.

| Intervention | Details | Perioperative caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Oxygen | Only if SpO2 below 90%: routine oxygen does not help and may harm (DETO2X-AMI, AVOID) | |
| Aspirin | 150 to 300 mg load, then 100 mg daily | Discuss with surgeon if fresh surgical bleeding |
| P2Y12 inhibitor | Ticagrelor 180 mg or prasugrel 60 mg load, or clopidogrel 300 to 600 mg (clopidogrel if fibrinolysis or oral anticoagulant or high bleeding risk) | Bleeding risk; cardiology decision |
| Anticoagulation | Unfractionated heparin (70 to 100 U/kg bolus) or enoxaparin | Fresh surgical site: individualised |
| Analgesia | Titrated IV opioid (fentanyl or morphine); morphine delays absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors | |
| Nitrates | GTN SL or IV for ongoing ischaemia, hypertension or pulmonary oedema | Avoid with SBP below 90, RV infarct, PDE-5 inhibitor within 24 to 48 h |
| Beta-blocker | IV only if tachycardic and hypertensive without heart failure or shock; early oral beta-blocker in stable patients | Avoid in shock, bradycardia, high-grade block, acute HF (COMMIT-CCS2: more cardiogenic shock with early IV metoprolol) |
| Statin | High-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg | |
| ACEi / ARB | Early in anterior MI, HF or LV dysfunction once stable | Avoid in shock or AKI |
| Antiemetic, anxiolytic | As needed | |

**Anaesthetic and perioperative modifications:** treat the cause (hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia, hypoxia), deepen anaesthesia or analgesia, maintain MAP (phenylephrine, noradrenaline), reduce HR, and escalate monitoring with invasive BP and TOE.

## 2.4 Reperfusion strategies

| Option | Indications and key points |
|---|---|
| Primary PCI | Preferred for STEMI; target first medical contact to wire crossing within 90 min (60 min if self-presenting to a PCI centre); within 120 min of diagnosis if transfer needed. Benefit up to 12 h from symptom onset; later if ongoing ischaemia, shock or arrhythmia |
| Fibrinolysis | If primary PCI cannot be achieved in 120 min: tenecteplase, alteplase or reteplase within 30 min of diagnosis; then transfer for angiography within 2 to 24 h (pharmaco-invasive strategy, STREAM). Rescue PCI if failed. **Absolute contraindications:** prior intracranial haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke within 3 months, known intracranial neoplasm or AVM, suspected aortic dissection, active bleeding, significant head or facial trauma in 3 months. **Perioperatively, major surgery within 3 weeks is a relative contraindication**, so PCI is preferred |
| Urgent angiography | NSTEMI with instability, refractory pain, haemodynamic or electrical instability, or heart failure (within 2 h); high-risk (GRACE above 140) within 24 h |
| CABG | Left main or three-vessel disease with diabetes, failed PCI, mechanical complications |

> **Figure (diagram not reproduced):** ACS reperfusion pathway · 1 decision, shock escalation. The ST-elevation decision drives reperfusion route and timing; cardiogenic shock overrides the pathway at any step.

## 2.5 Cardiogenic shock (SS_IC 1.31, SS_CS 1.26)

**Definition:** sustained hypotension (SBP below 90 mmHg for 30 min or vasopressors needed) with evidence of hypoperfusion (lactate above 2 mmol/L, cold peripheries, oliguria, altered mentation) and elevated filling pressures, caused by primary cardiac dysfunction. Cardiac index below 2.2 L/min/m2 with PCWP above 15 mmHg.

**Causes after MI:** pump failure (large infarct, 40% of LV loss), RV infarction, mechanical complications (acute severe MR from papillary muscle rupture, VSD, free wall rupture and tamponade), arrhythmia.

**SCAI staging:**

| Stage | Features |
|---|---|
| A At risk | Risk factors for shock; normal perfusion |
| B Beginning | Hypotension or tachycardia, no hypoperfusion |
| C Classic | Hypoperfusion requiring intervention (drugs, mechanical support); lactate often above 2 |
| D Deteriorating | Worsening despite initial support; escalation needed |
| E Extremis | Cardiac arrest or CPR, on multiple support devices |

**Management principles:**

- **Emergency revascularisation** of the culprit lesion is the key treatment (SHOCK trial: survival benefit at 6 and 12 months). Culprit-only PCI is preferred (CULPRIT-SHOCK).
- **Haemodynamics:** noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor (SOAP II: fewer arrhythmias than dopamine; better 28-day survival in the cardiogenic shock subgroup). Add adrenaline only if refractory (more arrhythmia and refractory shock). Dobutamine 2.5 to 10 micrograms/kg/min as the first-line inotrope; consider levosimendan or milrinone with caution (hypotension; milrinone renal clearance). Vasopressin as an adjunct to spare catecholamines.
- **Avoid excess fluid** (unless RV infarct or hypovolaemia). Cautious 250 mL boluses.
- **Respiratory support:** oxygen, high-flow, NIV or intubation. Anaesthetic induction in shock is dangerous (see below).
- **Mechanical circulatory support (MCS):** see 2.6.
- **Treat arrhythmia, acidosis, anaemia (MINT: liberal transfusion considered), electrolytes.** Avoid hypothermia unless post-arrest.
- **Monitoring:** arterial line, central venous access, serial lactate, ScvO2, echo, consider PA catheter to guide complex shock (PCWP, CO, PVR; the right ventricle matters).

**Haemodynamic profile (Forrester / Stevenson):**

| Profile | Perfusion | Congestion | Typical therapy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warm and dry | Adequate | No | Continue oral therapy |
| Warm and wet | Adequate | Yes | Diuretics, vasodilators |
| Cold and wet | Poor | Yes | Inotrope, vasopressor, MCS, diuretics |
| Cold and dry | Poor | No | Fluids, inotrope |

## 2.6 Mechanical circulatory support

| Device | Mechanism | Evidence | Key limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) | Counterpulsation in the descending aorta: inflates in diastole (raising diastolic pressure and coronary perfusion), deflates just before systole (reduces afterload, LV wall stress and O2 demand). Small rise in CO (about 0.5 L/min) | IABP-SHOCK II: no mortality benefit in MI shock; now class III in ESC/ACC | Aortic regurgitation, aortic dissection, severe peripheral vascular disease; works only with a rhythm that triggers and adequate native output; limb ischaemia, bleeding, thrombocytopenia |
| Impella (percutaneous LV assist, axial flow) | Pumps blood from LV to ascending aorta, giving up to 2.5 to 5.5 L/min depending on model | DanGer Shock (STEMI shock): lower 180-day mortality, more bleeding and limb ischaemia | Haemolysis, vascular complications, LV thrombus is a contraindication, mechanical aortic valve |
| VA-ECMO | Venous drainage to oxygenator and pump, return to femoral artery; full support (4 to 6 L/min) but raises LV afterload and can cause LV distension and pulmonary oedema unless vented (Impella, IABP, balloon septostomy) | ECLS-SHOCK, ECMO-CS: no mortality benefit in unselected shock | Bleeding, limb ischaemia, stroke, harlequin (differential hypoxia) syndrome, infection |
| TandemHeart / ECMO RV support | Right ventricular failure | Small series | |

**IABP waveform.** In the 1:2 assist mode the arterial trace alternates between an assisted and an unassisted beat. Features of a correct assisted beat: the **dicrotic notch** replaced by a sharp V-shaped inflation point; **diastolic augmentation** (peak above the systolic pressure); **assisted end-diastolic pressure** lower than unassisted end-diastolic; **assisted systolic pressure** lower than the unassisted systolic. Timing errors: early inflation (before the notch: aortic valve closes prematurely, reducing SV), late inflation (reduced augmentation), early deflation (loss of afterload reduction, 'U' shape), late deflation (balloon inflates against systole, increases afterload).

> **Figure (diagram not reproduced):** IABP 1:2 arterial pressure trace · points A to F. Compare the assisted and unassisted values: E should sit below A and F below B if counterpulsation is working.

**Physiological principle:** raising diastolic aortic pressure improves coronary perfusion (not in stenosed vessels where flow is fixed), and systolic unloading reduces LV wall tension, so oxygen supply rises while demand falls.

**Pitfall:** the IABP does not provide significant forward flow, so it does not help in profound shock or ventricular arrhythmia.

## 2.7 Anaesthesia for acute revascularisation (SS_CS 1.26)

**For primary PCI or emergency angiography:**

- Most patients can be managed with local anaesthetic and light sedation; the case for GA is airway protection in unstable patients with shock, cardiac arrest, respiratory failure or agitation.
- Avoid sedation that causes hypotension or hypoventilation.
- Consider the contrast load (renal), radiation and positioning.
- Reperfusion arrhythmias (accelerated idioventricular rhythm, VF), bleeding and vascular access complications are the major concerns.

**For emergency CABG (see Set 13 for CPB):**

- Preoperative: DAPT bleeding risk and platelet availability; stabilise with IABP or inotropes.
- Induction in shock: invasive arterial line before induction; titrate induction agent (etomidate or ketamine; reduced dose), maintain MAP with noradrenaline or vasopressin, avoid tachycardia and hypotension; fentanyl-based balanced anaesthesia. Anticipate low cardiac output at induction because sympatholysis unmasks reduced reserve.
- Hypotension at induction in a failing ventricle is treated with vasopressor and inotrope early, not fluid alone.

**For anaesthesia in patients with recent PCI or MI undergoing urgent non-cardiac surgery:** follow Topic 1 (antiplatelet continuation, high-risk perioperative environment, post-operative HDU, troponin surveillance).

## 2.8 Mechanical complications and RV infarction

| Complication | Timing | Features | Management |
|---|---|---|---|
| Papillary muscle rupture (acute severe MR) | 2 to 7 days (posteromedial papillary muscle, single blood supply: PDA) | Pulmonary oedema, shock, soft murmur because of equalised pressures, large v wave | Afterload reduction (nitroprusside), IABP, urgent surgery |
| Ventricular septal rupture | 3 to 5 days | New loud pansystolic murmur, left-to-right shunt, RV overload | IABP, surgical or percutaneous closure |
| Free wall rupture | 5 to 14 days | Tamponade, PEA | Pericardiocentesis, emergency surgery |
| RV infarction | With inferior MI | Hypotension, raised JVP, clear lungs | Fluids to preload optimum, inotropes, maintain AV synchrony, avoid nitrates and diuretics, pacing for AV block |
| Arrhythmia | Reperfusion; VT/VF within 48 h | | Defibrillation, amiodarone, correct K/Mg, beta-blocker |

## 2.9 After the acute event

DAPT for 12 months after ACS (shorter with high bleeding risk), high-intensity statin, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor or ARB, mineralocorticoid antagonist for LVEF 40% or less with HF or diabetes, cardiac rehabilitation, and secondary prevention. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator evaluation 40 days or more after MI and 3 months after revascularisation if LVEF stays 35% or less.

items.title: Describe how you approach hypertension before and during anaesthesia, including drugs for acute control.
items.sub: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.eyebrow: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.q: Describe how you approach hypertension before and during anaesthesia, including drugs for acute control.
items.a:
- Definitions: hypertension 140/90 or more; grade 3 at or above 180/110.
- Preoperative: below 180/110 proceed; at or above 180/110 consider deferring elective surgery for control; look for end-organ damage and secondary causes.
- Drug plan: continue most antihypertensives; omit diuretics; consider withholding ACEi/ARB.
- Intraoperative physiology: autoregulatory curve shifted right; exaggerated pressor and depressor response.
- Acute treatment: remove causes (pain, light anaesthesia, hypercapnia); esmolol, labetalol, GTN, hydralazine, nicardipine, clevidipine.
- Hypertensive emergency: lower MAP no more than 25% in the first hour.

> **Closing point:** Intraoperative hypotension is more harmful than mild hypertension.

items.title: 10. Anaesthetic induction in severe LV dysfunction or shock
items.q: You must anaesthetise a patient with an EF of 20% and marginal blood pressure for an emergency procedure. How do you prepare and induce?
items.a:
## 1. Physiological problem
- An EF of 20% means a severely reduced stroke volume, with a flat Starling curve, raised end-diastolic pressure and dependence on sympathetic tone and preload to maintain output.
- Induction agents reduce sympathetic tone, vasodilate (afterload falls, which can help the failing ventricle but may drop perfusion pressure), venodilate (preload falls) and depress contractility. Positive pressure ventilation reduces venous return and raises RV afterload.
- In low-output states, circulation time is prolonged, so IV drugs act slowly and overshoot is common, and drug requirements are reduced (induction doses may be a quarter to a third of normal).
- Marginal blood pressure means coronary perfusion is also at risk.

## 2. Preparation
- **Resuscitate:** optimise volume (cautious fluid, or diuresis if overloaded), correct electrolytes (potassium above 4, magnesium above 1) and acidosis, treat arrhythmia, and make sure pads are applied.
- **Establish the diagnosis:** ECG, echo (EF, RV, valves, tamponade), lactate, and the cause of shock (ischaemia, arrhythmia, drugs, sepsis).
- **Team and location:** senior anaesthetist, an assistant who can manage drugs, and a plan for failed intubation and arrest.
- **Consider whether surgery should proceed:** a less invasive alternative (local or regional technique, sedation) might be safer.
- **Mechanical support** (IABP, ECMO) should be discussed in advance if the patient is in extremis.

## 3. Monitoring and access
- Arterial line before induction (awake, under local anaesthetic) for beat-to-beat pressure.
- Large-bore IV access, central line with vasopressor infusion ready.
- ECG with ST analysis, SpO2, capnography, temperature, urine output.
- Cardiac output monitoring (pulse contour, oesophageal Doppler) or TOE for major surgery; a PA catheter if complex.

## 4. Induction technique
| Element | Choice and rationale |
|---|---|
| Preparation | Vasopressor (noradrenaline infusion, or phenylephrine and metaraminol boluses) running or drawn up; inotrope (adrenaline, dobutamine, milrinone) available |
| Preoxygenation | Careful, with head-up; high-flow nasal oxygen reduces desaturation |
| Agent | Etomidate (0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg) preserves haemodynamics (but adrenal suppression with repeated doses or in sepsis), ketamine (0.5 to 1 mg/kg; has intrinsic myocardial depression in catecholamine-depleted patients but maintains sympathetic tone), or a reduced and slowly titrated dose of propofol or midazolam with fentanyl |
| Opioid | Fentanyl or remifentanil in titrated dose; opioids provide haemodynamic stability |
| Muscle relaxant | Rocuronium (1 to 1.2 mg/kg for RSI); slower circulation delays onset |
| Technique | Modified rapid sequence or slow gentle induction depending on aspiration risk; avoid hypoxia and hypercapnia |

## 5. Maintenance and ventilation
- Titrate low-dose volatile or TIVA against depth monitoring (BIS), accepting the risk of awareness in shock; use ketamine or opioids to supplement.
- Positive pressure ventilation reduces venous return and increases RV afterload: use the lowest mean airway pressure, tidal volume of 6 to 8 mL/kg and modest PEEP.
- Maintain MAP above 65 (higher if chronic hypertension), sinus rhythm, and a normal to slightly high heart rate.
- Fluids: restrict or titrate to dynamic indices; transfuse for anaemia.
- Inotropes and vasopressors: noradrenaline, dobutamine, milrinone, vasopressin, as in R8.

## 6. Regional and neuraxial options
Peripheral nerve blocks and cautious epidural (slowly titrated) can avoid general anaesthesia, but a single-shot spinal causes abrupt sympathectomy and is dangerous in fixed low output states.

## 7. Postoperative
ICU or HDU, ongoing inotrope or vasopressor support, a plan for ventilation and weaning, and early mechanical support if refractory.

> **Examiner lens:** pre-empt the induction hypotension with vasopressors, not fluid alone.

items.title: List the principles of managing acute RV failure.
items.sub: 6. Cardiomyopathy
items.eyebrow: 6. Cardiomyopathy
items.q: List the principles of managing acute RV failure.
items.a:
- Causes: pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension, RV infarct, ARDS, LVAD, cardiomyopathy, valve disease.
- Reduce RV afterload: oxygen, avoid hypoxia, acidosis, hypercarbia, hypothermia; inhaled nitric oxide or epoprostenol, sildenafil, milrinone.
- Preserve RV perfusion: noradrenaline or vasopressin to keep MAP well above PA pressure.
- Optimise preload: avoid both hypovolaemia and overload; diurese if distended.
- Support contractility: dobutamine, milrinone.
- Keep sinus rhythm; low airway pressures.
- Mechanical: RVAD, VA-ECMO.

> **Closing point:** The RV needs pressure and low PVR, not just volume.

items.title: List the initial medical management of ACS.
items.sub: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.eyebrow: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.q: List the initial medical management of ACS.
items.a:
- Monitor, 12-lead ECG, analgesia as needed, oxygen only if SpO2 below 90% (AVOID, DETO2X).
- Aspirin 150 to 300 mg load.
- P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or prasugrel preferred) per cardiology.
- Anticoagulant: UFH, enoxaparin or bivalirudin.
- GTN for ongoing pain or hypertension (avoid with hypotension, RV infarct, PDE5 inhibitors).
- Beta-blocker if no heart failure, shock or heart block.
- High-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor, and later mineralocorticoid antagonist if EF 40% or less.
- Risk stratify (GRACE, TIMI); early invasive strategy in high risk.

> **Closing point:** Treat the culprit early with reperfusion, not just drugs.

items.title: 16. Mechanical valves, anticoagulation and pregnancy
items.q: Describe how you manage anticoagulation for a patient with a mechanical mitral valve having elective surgery, and how the problem changes in pregnancy.
items.a:
## 1. Thromboembolic risk of mechanical valves
- **Without anticoagulation** the risk of valve thrombosis and systemic embolism is about 4% per year for aortic valves and 8% for mitral valves (higher with caged-ball or tilting disc designs).
- **Risk stratification (ACC/AHA, ESC, CHEST/ACCP):**
- **Low risk:** bileaflet mechanical aortic valve without risk factors.
- **Intermediate:** bileaflet aortic valve with one risk factor (AF, previous thromboembolism, LV dysfunction with EF below 35%, hypercoagulable state, older-generation valve).
- **High:** any mechanical mitral valve, caged-ball or tilting disc aortic valve, recent stroke or TIA (within 6 months), or an aortic valve with multiple risk factors.
- **INR targets:** bileaflet aortic with no risk factors 2.5 (2.0 to 3.0); mechanical aortic with risk factors, and mechanical mitral or tricuspid 3.0 (2.5 to 3.5).
- DOACs are contraindicated (RE-ALIGN: dabigatran caused more thromboembolism and bleeding; PROACT Xa: apixaban was stopped for excess thromboembolism). Warfarin is the only recommended oral agent.

## 2. Perioperative plan
| Step | Management |
|---|---|
| Preoperative assessment | Valve type and position, INR target, other risk factors, bleeding risk of the procedure, and renal function. For minor procedures (dental, cataract, minor skin) warfarin can be continued with INR in range |
| Stopping warfarin | Stop 5 days before surgery (INR 1.5 or below for most major surgery; INR below 1.4 or normal for neuraxial block), with INR check the day before. Low-dose oral vitamin K (1 to 2 mg) may be used if INR is still above 1.5 the day before |
| Bridging | Indicated for high-risk valves (mechanical mitral, caged-ball, tilting disc, recent stroke, AF with multiple risk factors). Start therapeutic LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily) or IV UFH when INR is below 2.0 (about day 3 before surgery); the last LMWH dose is given 24 hours before surgery (half the daily dose in some protocols), UFH stopped 4 to 6 hours before. Not required for low-risk bileaflet aortic valves |
| Evidence | BRIDGE (1884 patients with AF) found that no bridging was non-inferior for thromboembolism and caused less major bleeding, but mechanical valves were excluded; the data for mechanical valves are therefore observational and expert-based |
| Postoperative | Restart warfarin within 12 to 24 hours of surgery (evening of the operation if haemostasis is secure), with LMWH 48 to 72 hours after major surgery with high bleeding risk (24 hours after low bleeding risk), until INR is therapeutic |
| Neuraxial block | Wait for INR below 1.4; wait 12 hours (prophylactic dose) or 24 hours (therapeutic dose) after LMWH before needle placement; catheter removal timing per ANZCA PG/ASRA guidelines |

## 3. Emergency surgery or bleeding
- Reverse with prothrombin complex concentrate (25 to 50 units/kg, based on INR) plus vitamin K 5 to 10 mg IV for life-threatening bleeding; fresh frozen plasma is a second-line option.
- Vitamin K in high doses can delay re-anticoagulation for days, so lower doses (1 to 2 mg) are used for non-life-threatening cases.
- Resume anticoagulation as soon as the bleeding has been controlled.

## 4. Pregnancy
- **Problem:** pregnancy is hypercoagulable, and the options all carry risk.
- **Warfarin:** the most effective at preventing valve thrombosis, but crosses the placenta, causing embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses; risk of about 6% at 6 to 12 weeks, dose-dependent, higher above 5 mg/day), fetal bleeding and miscarriage.
- **LMWH or UFH:** do not cross the placenta, but are less effective at preventing valve thrombosis (up to 5 to 10% in mitral valves) and have monitoring challenges (anti-Xa levels, aPTT) with changing weight and renal clearance.
- **Strategy (ESC 2018 and 2021; ACC/AHA):**
- Informed shared decision-making before conception, in a pregnancy heart team.
- If the warfarin dose is 5 mg/day or less: continue warfarin through the first trimester (lowest risk of valve thrombosis) or switch to LMWH twice daily with anti-Xa monitoring between 6 and 12 weeks if the patient prefers; if above 5 mg/day, use LMWH or UFH in the first trimester.
- Warfarin from week 13 to about week 36.
- Switch to LMWH or IV UFH from week 36 (or earlier if labour is anticipated) because of fetal bleeding risk and to permit regional anaesthesia.
- Stop LMWH 24 hours before planned induction or caesarean section; use IV UFH, stopped 4 to 6 hours before delivery. Restart 6 to 12 hours after vaginal delivery (UFH or LMWH) and warfarin once bleeding is controlled.
- If delivery occurs on warfarin, an urgent caesarean section is advised (neonatal intracranial haemorrhage), with vitamin K and PCC.
- **Anaesthetic implications:** delivery planning in a tertiary centre; neuraxial analgesia in labour is possible if the INR and heparin timings are met; careful haemodynamic monitoring (increased volume, MS and AF risk).

## 5. Key messages
Know the INR targets, who needs bridging, the avoidance of DOACs, and the trade-off between maternal valve thrombosis and fetal harm in pregnancy.

> **Examiner lens:** know the INR targets, who needs bridging, and the trade-off in pregnancy.

items.title: Classify heart failure.
items.sub: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.eyebrow: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.q: Classify heart failure.
items.a:
- By ejection fraction: HFrEF 40% or less, HFmrEF 41 to 49%, HFpEF 50% or more.
- By time course: acute, chronic, acute-on-chronic.
- By side: left, right, biventricular.
- By output: low-output versus high-output (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, AV fistula, sepsis, Paget disease).
- Functional: NYHA I to IV.
- Structural: ACC/AHA stages A to D.
- Profile: warm/cold and wet/dry.

> **Closing point:** HFpEF is about half of all heart failure and is not benign.

items.title: 11. HFrEF patient on full therapy for elective surgery
items.q: A 65-year-old with HFrEF (EF 30%) on sacubitril-valsartan, bisoprolol, spironolactone and dapagliflozin is booked for elective major surgery. How do you manage his medications, fluids and monitoring?
items.a:
## 1. Assess whether he is optimised
- **Clinical status:** NYHA class, symptoms, weight trend, peripheral oedema, JVP, orthopnoea, recent hospitalisation. Decompensated HF is a reason to defer elective surgery (it is associated with a several-fold increase in mortality).
- **Investigations:** ECG, echo (EF, RV function, valves, filling pressures; repeat if clinical change or echo older than 12 months), BNP or NT-proBNP (a high or rising value signals risk), electrolytes (potassium, magnesium), renal function, FBC, and glucose.
- **Risk:** HFrEF with an EF of 30% is a strong predictor of perioperative HF, AKI, and death (an RCRI point, and 30 day mortality of about 10% in major surgery).
- **Team:** cardiology input, heart failure nurse, and a decision on location (HDU).

## 2. Medications
| Drug | Perioperative approach | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Beta-blocker (bisoprolol) | Continue, including on the morning | Withdrawal causes tachycardia, ischaemia and arrhythmia |
| ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan), ACEi, ARB | Commonly omitted on the morning of surgery (24 hours for ARNI), restarted when haemodynamically stable. ARNI has a longer duration and more vasodilation; some centres continue in stable HFrEF | Vasoplegia, hypotension under anaesthesia (STOP-or-NOT found no difference in composite outcome) |
| MRA (spironolactone) | Continue if stable, or withhold the morning dose if poor intake, renal impairment or hyperkalaemia | Hyperkalaemia, AKI |
| SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin) | Stop 3 days before (3 to 4 days; ANZCA/ADS and FDA advice) | Euglycaemic ketoacidosis in fasted, stressed patients |
| Loop diuretic | Omit on the morning if euvolaemic; continue if congested | Avoid hypovolaemia and electrolyte disturbance |
| Digoxin, amiodarone, ivabradine | Continue | Rhythm and rate control |
| Anticoagulants | Per indication (AF, LV thrombus) | Bridging only if high thrombotic risk |

Restart all drugs as soon as the patient is eating and haemodynamically stable, and review within 48 hours.

## 3. Device
Check the ICD or CRT status and interrogation, and plan for diathermy (see R21).

## 4. Anaesthetic plan
- **Technique:** a technique that preserves haemodynamics. Regional or neuraxial for suitable surgery (slowly titrated); general anaesthesia with titrated agents (see R10).
- **Monitoring:** invasive arterial pressure, cardiac output monitoring or TOE for major surgery, ST analysis, urine output, temperature. Consider a central line for vasopressors.
- **Induction:** vasopressor ready, reduced doses, opioid-based.
- **Haemodynamic goals:** see R12 (preload maintained but not excessive, afterload low-normal with adequate MAP, contractility supported, rate normal to high-normal, sinus rhythm).
- **Ventilation:** lung-protective ventilation, modest PEEP, avoid hypoxia and hypercarbia (raised PVR).

## 5. Fluids
- Both hypovolaemia and overload are poorly tolerated. A goal-directed strategy (stroke volume or cardiac output guided, with dynamic indices or echo) is preferred to fixed volumes. Use balanced crystalloid in modest amounts; replace blood loss with blood. In HFrEF, pulse pressure variation and SVV have lower reliability with arrhythmias and low tidal volumes.
- Consider early vasopressor or inotrope rather than repeated fluid boluses.

## 6. Postoperative
- HDU for major surgery, with continuous ECG and invasive BP.
- Early extubation if possible; multimodal analgesia (avoid NSAIDs: fluid retention, renal injury).
- Daily weights and fluid balance, repeat BNP or troponin, restart GDMT, and treat precipitants (arrhythmia, ischaemia, anaemia, infection).
- Early recognition of decompensation (see R14) and VTE prophylaxis.

> **Examiner lens:** know which drugs to hold (SGLT2i, ARNI/ACEi morning), which to continue (beta-blocker) and why.

items.title: List the ways of detecting intraoperative myocardial ischaemia and their limits.
items.sub: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.eyebrow: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.q: List the ways of detecting intraoperative myocardial ischaemia and their limits.
items.a:
- ECG: lead II plus V5 detects about 80% of ischaemia; V4 plus V5 about 90%; use diagnostic mode; ST depression of 1 mm at 60 to 80 ms after the J point.
- Limits of ECG: LBBB, paced rhythm, digoxin, LVH, posterior and circumflex ischaemia may be silent.
- TOE: new regional wall motion abnormality, an earlier sign than ECG; transgastric mid short-axis view.
- Haemodynamic signs: hypotension, arrhythmia, rising PAOP with large v waves (late sign).
- Biomarkers: postoperative troponin surveillance.
- Symptoms are masked under general anaesthesia.

> **Closing point:** Most perioperative infarction is silent, so use surveillance.

items.title: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.los: IT_PO 1.4 (left heart failure component); SS_CS 1.4 (filling status; LV systolic and diastolic function); SS_IC 1.35 (heart failure in intensive care)
items.body:
## 3.1 Definitions and classification

**Heart failure (HF):** clinical syndrome of symptoms and signs caused by structural or functional cardiac abnormality, with raised natriuretic peptides or objective evidence of congestion.

| Type | LVEF | Features |
|---|---|---|
| HFrEF | 40% or less | Systolic dysfunction; dilated LV, reduced contractility |
| HFmrEF | 41 to 49% | Intermediate; treat like HFrEF if symptomatic (ESC 2023) |
| HFpEF | 50% or more | Diastolic dysfunction, LVH, raised filling pressures, LA enlargement; often elderly, hypertensive, diabetic, obese, women |
| HFimpEF | Baseline 40% or less, improved by 10 points to above 40% | Continue therapy |

**Staging:** ACC/AHA stages A to D (A at risk, B structural disease without symptoms, C symptomatic, D refractory). **NYHA class I to IV** by symptoms: I no limitation; II slight, symptoms on ordinary activity; III marked, symptoms on less than ordinary activity; IV symptoms at rest.

**Acute HF presentations:** acute decompensated chronic HF (most), acute pulmonary oedema, cardiogenic shock, hypertensive HF, isolated right HF.

## 3.2 Pathophysiology

- **Systolic dysfunction:** reduced contractility and ejection. Low stroke volume activates the sympathetic nervous system (tachycardia, vasoconstriction), RAAS (sodium and water retention, afterload), and natriuretic peptide release. Chronic activation causes remodelling: eccentric hypertrophy, dilatation, functional MR, and arrhythmia.
- **Diastolic dysfunction:** impaired relaxation (active, energy-dependent early diastole) and increased stiffness (passive compliance). The LV pressure-volume curve shifts up and left: small volume changes cause large pressure changes. Atrial contraction contributes 30 to 40% of filling (instead of 15 to 20%), so AF and tachycardia are badly tolerated.

| Feature | Systolic dysfunction | Diastolic dysfunction |
|---|---|---|
| End-systolic pressure-volume relationship | Shifted down and right (reduced Ees) | Normal |
| End-diastolic pressure-volume relationship | Shifted right (dilated) | Shifted up and left (stiff) |
| EDV | Increased | Normal or reduced |
| EF | Reduced | Preserved |
| Preload response | Plateaus on a flat Starling curve | Steep: small volume changes cause large pressure swings |
| Poorly tolerated | Afterload rise, negative inotropes | Tachycardia, AF, hypovolaemia and hypervolaemia, ischaemia |

## 3.3 Perioperative assessment of LV function and filling status (SS_CS 1.4)

**Clinical:** orthopnoea, PND, oedema, JVP, S3 gallop, crepitations, hepatomegaly, ascites, cool peripheries, exercise tolerance (NYHA, DASI).

**Investigations:**

| Test | Value |
|---|---|
| BNP / NT-proBNP | Rule-out value (BNP below 100 ng/L, NT-proBNP below 300 ng/L); raised by age, renal failure, AF and falls with obesity. Preoperative level predicts MACE (see Topic 1) |
| ECG | Ischaemia, LBBB (dyssynchrony), AF, LVH, QRS duration for CRT |
| CXR | Cardiomegaly, upper-lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, effusions |
| Echo | LVEF (biplane Simpson), regional wall motion, valves, filling pressures, RV function, pulmonary pressures |
| Cardiac MRI, nuclear | Viability, aetiology, EF |
| Invasive | PA catheter data for complex cases |

**Echo assessment of LV systolic function:**

| Parameter | Normal / cut-off |
|---|---|
| LVEF (ASE) | 52 to 72% men, 54 to 74% women; mildly reduced 41 to 51 / 41 to 53 |
| Fractional shortening | 25 to 43% |
| Global longitudinal strain | Normal about -18 to -20% or more negative; a better marker than EF |
| Fractional area change (mid-papillary SAX) | Above 35% (TOE) |
| Qualitative on FoCUS | Normal, mildly, moderately or severely reduced; interventricular septum motion |
| Dimensions | LV end-diastolic diameter 3.9 to 5.3 cm (women), 4.2 to 5.9 cm (men) |

**Echo assessment of diastolic function (ASE/EACVI 2016 algorithm):** four criteria for diastolic dysfunction: annular e' (septal below 7 cm/s or lateral below 10 cm/s), average E/e' above 14, LA volume index above 34 mL/m2, and TR velocity above 2.8 m/s. If more than half are abnormal, diastolic dysfunction is present; if half, indeterminate.

| Grade | E/A | E/e' | Other | LAP |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Normal | 0.8 to 2 | Below 8 to 10 | | Normal |
| I (impaired relaxation) | Below 0.8 | Below 10 | E below 50 cm/s | Normal or low |
| II (pseudonormal) | 0.8 to 2 | 10 to 14 | Valsalva changes E/A (decrease by 0.5 or more), LAVI above 34 | Raised |
| III (restrictive) | Above 2 | Above 14 | Short DT below 160 ms, IVRT below 70 ms | Markedly raised |

**Assessment of filling status and fluid responsiveness (see Set 10 for the underlying haemodynamics):** CVP and PAOP are poor predictors of volume responsiveness. Better: dynamic tests (passive leg raise, SVV and PPV with caveats of tidal volume above 8 mL/kg and sinus rhythm), IVC diameter and collapsibility (diameter 2.1 cm or less with collapse above 50% suggests RAP about 3 mmHg), LVOT VTI change, and E/e' for filling pressure. In HF, fluid challenges should be small (250 mL) and reassessed.

## 3.4 Chronic management of HF (basis of perioperative continuation)

| Drug class | Role | Perioperative note |
|---|---|---|
| ACEi / ARB / ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan) | Mortality benefit in HFrEF (SOLVD, PARADIGM-HF) | Hold morning of surgery in most; omit ARNI 36 h before if switching to ACEi; hypotension risk with anaesthesia |
| Beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) | Mortality benefit (CIBIS-II, MERIT-HF, COPERNICUS) | Continue; avoid abrupt withdrawal |
| MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone) | RALES, EPHESUS | Check K and renal function |
| SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) | DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced; EMPEROR-Preserved and DELIVER in HFpEF | **Withhold 3 to 4 days before surgery** (euglycaemic ketoacidosis) |
| Loop diuretics | Symptom control | Omit morning dose if euvolaemic; resume early |
| Ivabradine | SHIFT: HR above 70 despite beta-blocker | Continue |
| Digoxin | Symptoms and rate control | Check level, K |
| Hydralazine plus nitrate | For African ancestry (A-HeFT) and ACEi intolerance | |
| Device therapy | ICD (primary prevention LVEF 35% or less), CRT (LBBB, QRS 150 ms or more) | Reprogramme perioperatively (see device guidance in Set 12) |

## 3.5 Anaesthetic implications and perioperative risk (IT_PO 1.4)

HF is a major independent predictor of perioperative mortality, MACE, readmission and prolonged stay. Elective surgery should be deferred if decompensated; optimise euvolaemia and GDMT beforehand.

**Haemodynamic goals:**

| Systolic dysfunction | Diastolic dysfunction |
|---|---|
| Preload: maintain but avoid overload | Preload: maintain, adequate filling is crucial |
| Afterload: low to normal (avoid vasoconstriction; vasodilators help) | Afterload: avoid large rises |
| Heart rate: normal to high-normal (CO depends on HR in a fixed SV state; avoid bradycardia) | Heart rate: slow (50 to 80) to maximise filling time |
| Rhythm: keep sinus rhythm | **Sinus rhythm is critical**; treat AF early (cardioversion if unstable) |
| Contractility: support with inotrope if needed; avoid negative inotropes | Contractility: preserved; avoid excess inotropy |
| Avoid | Avoid tachycardia, ischaemia, hypervolaemia |

**Anaesthetic technique:**

- Choose agents with minimal myocardial depression: etomidate or ketamine (with caution) or slow-titrated propofol for induction; opioid-based, balanced technique; volatile agents are acceptable at low MAC.
- Invasive arterial monitoring before induction for severe LV dysfunction; consider cardiac output monitoring and TOE.
- Vasopressor (noradrenaline) infusion ready before induction; inotrope (dobutamine, adrenaline) or milrinone if low output; vasopressin for vasodilatory states.
- Neuraxial anaesthesia can be well tolerated in compensated HF (controlled onset, slow titration of epidural or CSE; sympathetic block reduces afterload) but severe aortic stenosis or fixed output states are an exception. Maintain MAP with vasopressors. Monitor ECG, SpO2 and blood pressure (arterial line for severe dysfunction), and watch for signs of fluid overload or pulmonary oedema throughout.
- Fluids: restrictive and goal-directed; avoid large crystalloid loads; treat blood loss with blood.
- Postoperative: HDU, early extubation where possible, repeat BNP or troponin, fluid balance, restart GDMT.

## 3.6 Heart failure in the intensive care unit (SS_IC 1.35)

**Aim:** treat the cause, relieve congestion, restore perfusion, and protect organs.

**Initial assessment:** perfusion and congestion profile (warm/cold, wet/dry; see Topic 2); ECG, troponin, BNP, lactate, echo, CXR. Identify precipitants using the mnemonic **CHAMP**: acute **C** oronary syndrome, **H** ypertensive emergency, **A** rrhythmia, acute **M** echanical cause (valve, VSD, rupture), **P** ulmonary embolism. Others: infection, non-adherence, anaemia, thyroid, drugs (NSAIDs, negative inotropes), fluid overload, renal failure.

**Treatment:**

| Goal | Therapy |
|---|---|
| Oxygenation and breathing | Oxygen if SpO2 below 90%; CPAP or NIV for pulmonary oedema (see Topic 5); intubate for exhaustion, shock or failure of NIV |
| Decongestion | IV loop diuretic: furosemide 20 to 40 mg IV bolus (or 1 to 2.5 times the oral dose), infusion if inadequate. DOSE trial: high-dose (2.5 times) vs low-dose and bolus vs infusion gave similar symptom outcomes, with more transient creatinine rise at high dose. Add thiazide (metolazone) or acetazolamide (ADVOR) for resistance; ultrafiltration if refractory |
| Vasodilators | GTN or nitroprusside for hypertensive, congested patients with SBP above 110 (benefit mainly in APO) |
| Perfusion (low-output state) | Dobutamine 2.5 to 20 micrograms/kg/min; milrinone 0.125 to 0.5 micrograms/kg/min (no loading dose in hypotension); levosimendan (calcium sensitiser, vasodilator; SURVIVE and REVIVE mixed results); noradrenaline to maintain MAP above 65; vasopressin |
| Mechanical support | IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO as a bridge to recovery, device or transplant (see Topic 2.6). ECMO also treats refractory VF/cardiac arrest (ECPR) |
| Rhythm | Cardioversion for unstable tachyarrhythmias; amiodarone; pacing for bradycardia |
| Renal and metabolic | Correct K and Mg; monitor creatinine (cardiorenal syndrome); renal replacement or ultrafiltration if needed |
| Other | Venous thromboprophylaxis, nutrition, early mobilisation, palliative care input in advanced HF |

**Pulmonary artery catheter in HF:** ESCAPE showed no benefit of routine PAC-guided therapy in acute decompensated HF, so reserve it for shock of uncertain mechanism, refractory shock, transplant or LVAD assessment and pulmonary hypertension.

**Cardiogenic shock after non-ischaemic causes:** myocarditis, takotsubo, peripartum cardiomyopathy, decompensated chronic HF, drug toxicity. Same principles; VA-ECMO is a bridge to recovery (for example fulminant myocarditis).

**Advanced HF therapies:** LVAD (HeartMate 3, destination therapy or bridge to transplant), heart transplant. Anaesthetic considerations for the LVAD patient: no pulse (use arterial line and MAP, the Doppler MAP), preload and RV function dependence, anticoagulated, driveline infection, and pump thrombosis. Avoid hypovolaemia, high PVR, and tachyarrhythmia.

items.title: Describe how aortic stenosis is graded and what echo findings you quote.
items.sub: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.eyebrow: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.q: Describe how aortic stenosis is graded and what echo findings you quote.
items.a:
- Causes: senile calcific, bicuspid, rheumatic.
- Severe AS: Vmax 4 m/s or more, mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, AVA below 1.0 cm2 (indexed below 0.6 cm2/m2), dimensionless index below 0.25.
- Low-flow low-gradient (stroke volume index below 35 mL/m2): classic with low EF (use dobutamine stress echo) or paradoxical with preserved EF; calcium score on CT helps.
- Symptoms: angina, syncope, dyspnoea; survival falls to about 2 to 3 years once symptomatic.
- Treatment: SAVR or TAVI; balloon valvuloplasty as a bridge.

> **Closing point:** The AVA from the continuity equation depends on flow, so interpret gradients with stroke volume.

items.title: Describe the pathophysiology of AR and the haemodynamic goals.
items.sub: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.eyebrow: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.q: Describe the pathophysiology of AR and the haemodynamic goals.
items.a:
- Causes: annular dilation (hypertension, aortic root disease, Marfan), bicuspid valve, rheumatic, endocarditis, dissection.
- Chronic AR: volume overload, eccentric hypertrophy, wide pulse pressure; acute AR: no time to adapt, pulmonary oedema and shock.
- Severity: vena contracta above 6 mm, regurgitant volume 60 mL or more, pressure half-time below 200 ms, holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta.
- Goals: preload full, afterload low to normal (avoid vasoconstriction), heart rate high-normal 80 to 100 (shortens diastole and regurgitant time), contractility maintained.
- Avoid bradycardia, high SVR; IABP is contraindicated.

> **Closing point:** The opposite of AS: keep the heart faster and the afterload lower.

items.title: 17. Acute pulmonary oedema: cardiogenic versus non-cardiogenic
items.q: A postoperative patient develops acute pulmonary oedema. How do you determine the cause and what is your management for each major cause?
items.a:
## 1. Pathophysiology: Starling forces
Fluid filtration across the pulmonary capillary follows Starling: net flow = Kf x [(Pc - Pi) - sigma x (pi_c - pi_i)]. Oedema develops when capillary hydrostatic pressure rises, plasma oncotic pressure falls, capillary permeability increases, or lymphatic drainage is overwhelmed (the lymphatics can increase flow roughly 10-fold). Alveolar flooding follows interstitial oedema.

## 2. Immediate management for any cause (first minutes)
- Sit the patient upright, high-flow oxygen, and monitor (ECG, SpO2, NIBP; arterial line if unstable).
- IV access, ABG, 12-lead ECG, CXR, bedside echo and lung ultrasound, BNP and troponin.
- Early CPAP (5 to 10 cmH2O) or NIV for respiratory distress; 3CPO showed faster symptomatic improvement.
- Look for and treat the trigger.

## 3. Determining the cause
| Feature | Cardiogenic | Non-cardiogenic (permeability) |
|---|---|---|
| History | Cardiac disease, MI, arrhythmia, fluid overload, hypertension | Sepsis, aspiration, transfusion, pancreatitis, trauma, burns |
| Examination | Raised JVP, S3, cold or warm peripheries, peripheral oedema | Fever, normal JVP, warm |
| CXR | Cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, septal lines, perihilar bat-wing shadowing, effusions, wide vascular pedicle | Normal heart size, peripheral or patchy infiltrates, air bronchograms |
| BNP / NT-proBNP | Raised (BNP above 400 pg/mL) | Low to mildly raised (BNP below 100 argues against) |
| Echo | Reduced EF, valve disease, high E/e', dilated LA | Often normal LV |
| PAOP | Above 18 mmHg | Below 18 mmHg |
| Response to diuresis | Prompt | Poor |

Mixed pictures are common.

## 4. Management by mechanism
- **Cardiogenic:** GTN (sublingual or IV 5 to 200 micrograms/min) if SBP is above 100 mmHg, loop diuretic (furosemide 40 mg IV), treat ischaemia, arrhythmia (cardioversion), hypertension, valve failure (see R8, R14); inotropes if low output; avoid opioids.
- **TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload):** hypertension, raised JVP, raised BNP, positive fluid balance, responds to diuresis; slow transfusion in at-risk patients.
- **TRALI:** within 6 hours of transfusion, hypoxaemia, bilateral infiltrates, hypotension, fever, normal or low BNP; supportive (oxygen, lung-protective ventilation), no diuretics unless volume overloaded; notify the blood service and quarantine donor components.
- **ARDS:** Berlin criteria (acute, bilateral opacities, PaO2/FiO2 300 or below with PEEP at least 5, not fully explained by cardiac failure); lung-protective ventilation (6 mL/kg PBW, plateau below 30), prone position for P/F below 150 (PROSEVA), conservative fluid.
- **Negative pressure pulmonary oedema (NPPE):** after forceful inspiration against an obstructed airway (laryngospasm, strangulation, tumour); type 1 (acute obstruction) typically in young fit patients, type 2 after relief of chronic obstruction. Treat by relieving the obstruction, oxygen, CPAP or PEEP, and diuretics only if overloaded; it usually resolves in 12 to 48 hours.
- **Neurogenic oedema** (subarachnoid haemorrhage, head injury): catecholamine surge; treat the intracranial problem, support ventilation.
- **High altitude and re-expansion:** descent, oxygen, nifedipine; slow re-expansion of the lung.
- **Other:** anaphylaxis (adrenaline), pancreatitis, drug overdose (opioids, salicylates), pre-eclampsia.

## 5. Respiratory support
- Non-invasive support first if the patient is cooperative.
- Intubation for exhaustion, hypoxia refractory to CPAP, acidosis, or reduced consciousness: preoxygenate with CPAP, induction with ketamine or etomidate, vasopressor ready (venodilation and loss of sympathetic drive can cause collapse), PEEP of 8 to 12 cmH2O, avoid high volumes.

## 6. Summary
Stabilise oxygenation, work out the mechanism using the clinical features, BNP and echo, and give mechanism-specific therapy.

> **Examiner lens:** structure by mechanism (pressure, permeability, oncotic, negative pressure) and treat the mechanism.

items.sub: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.eyebrow: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.q: Contrast systolic and diastolic dysfunction.
items.a:
- Systolic: reduced contractility, dilated LV, EF low; flat Starling curve; causes include ischaemia, DCM, myocarditis.
- Diastolic: impaired relaxation and compliance, normal EF, steep end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship; causes include hypertension, ageing, LVH, diabetes, ischaemia, amyloid.
- Diastolic physiology: small volume changes cause large pressure changes; atrial kick contributes more; tachycardia and AF reduce filling.
- Clinical: both give breathlessness and oedema; diastolic failure can still present with pulmonary oedema.
- Echo: EF, wall thickness, E/A, e', E/e', LA size.

> **Closing point:** Diastolic failure is a pressure problem, so avoid tachycardia and loss of sinus rhythm.

items.title: Name the four pillars of HFrEF therapy and say how you handle each perioperatively.
items.sub: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.eyebrow: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.q: Name the four pillars of HFrEF therapy and say how you handle each perioperatively.
items.a:
- ARNI, ACEi or ARB (PARADIGM-HF; sacubitril-valsartan reduced death and HF admission versus enalapril): consider holding on the morning of surgery.
- Beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate): continue.
- Mineralocorticoid antagonist (RALES, EMPHASIS-HF): check K and renal function; hold on the day if poor intake.
- SGLT2 inhibitor (DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced): hold 3 to 4 days (euglycaemic ketoacidosis).
- Others: loop diuretic for symptoms, ivabradine, hydralazine plus nitrate, digoxin, CRT or ICD.
- Restart the pillars as soon as the patient is stable after surgery.

> **Closing point:** Every pillar improves survival, so restart early.

items.title: Explain how the intra-aortic balloon pump works and how you read the 1:2 trace.
items.sub: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.eyebrow: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.q: Explain how the intra-aortic balloon pump works and how you read the 1:2 trace.
items.a:
- Position: tip just below the left subclavian artery, above the renal arteries; helium (low density, rapid shuttling).
- Inflation at the dicrotic notch (start of diastole): raises diastolic pressure, improving coronary perfusion.
- Deflation just before systole: lowers end-diastolic pressure and afterload, reducing LV work.
- Effects: increased diastolic augmentation, lowered end-diastolic pressure and assisted systolic pressure, better coronary flow.
- 1:2 trace: assisted beat has a lower systolic and end-diastolic pressure than the unassisted beat; the augmented diastolic peak should exceed the systolic peak.
- Timing errors: early inflation (premature aortic valve closure), late inflation (lost augmentation), early deflation (lost afterload benefit), late deflation (increased afterload).
- Complications: limb ischaemia, aortic injury, balloon rupture (blood in tubing), thrombocytopenia, infection.

> **Closing point:** Inflate at the dicrotic notch and deflate before systole.

items.title: State the criteria for acute MI and map ECG leads to coronary territories.
items.sub: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.eyebrow: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.q: State the criteria for acute MI and map ECG leads to coronary territories.
items.a:
- Fourth Universal Definition: troponin rise and/or fall with at least one value above the 99th percentile plus one of symptoms, new ischaemic ECG change, pathological Q waves, imaging of new loss of viable myocardium or RWMA, or thrombus on angiography.
- Type 1 (plaque rupture), type 2 (supply-demand mismatch), type 3 (death before biomarkers), types 4 and 5 (PCI and CABG related).
- STEMI: new ST elevation at the J point of 1 mm in two contiguous leads (2 mm V2 to V3 in men 40 or over).
- Territories: anterior V1 to V4 (LAD); lateral I, aVL, V5 to V6 (LAD diagonal or LCx); inferior II, III, aVF (RCA 80%, LCx 20%); posterior tall R V1 to V3 (use V7 to V9); RV V4R.
- STEMI equivalents: de Winter, Wellens, posterior MI, new LBBB with Sgarbossa criteria, left main occlusion (aVR elevation).

> **Closing point:** Type 2 MI is common after surgery and is treated by correcting the imbalance.

items.title: List the mechanical complications of MI and their typical features.
items.sub: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.eyebrow: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.q: List the mechanical complications of MI and their typical features.
items.a:
- Free wall rupture: days 3 to 7, tamponade, PEA; surgical emergency.
- Ventricular septal rupture: harsh pansystolic murmur, left-to-right shunt, step-up in saturation.
- Papillary muscle rupture: acute severe MR, flash pulmonary oedema, soft murmur; posteromedial muscle in inferior MI.
- LV aneurysm and pseudoaneurysm; thrombus formation.
- RV infarction: hypotension with clear lungs, raised JVP; fluid, avoid nitrates.
- Others: arrhythmias, heart block, pericarditis (Dressler).
- Management: echo, afterload reduction, IABP, urgent surgery or percutaneous closure.

> **Closing point:** A new murmur and shock after MI is a mechanical complication until proven otherwise.

items.title: 7. Chest pain and ST elevation in PACU
items.q: A 70-year-old man 2 hours after radical prostatectomy has crushing chest pain, BP 90/50, HR 110 and widespread anterior ST elevation. Describe your immediate management and treatment priorities.
items.a:
## 1. Immediate response (the first 5 minutes)
- Call for help: the PACU team, anaesthetic senior, and the on-call cardiologist. Move to a monitored resuscitation space with defibrillator pads attached.
- Standard monitoring, large-bore IV access, supplemental oxygen only if SpO2 is below 90% (AVOID, DETO2X), a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, bedside echocardiography, and bloods (troponin, FBC, electrolytes, renal function, coagulation, group and screen, gas).
- Analgesia: titrated IV opioid (fentanyl), with caution because of hypotension.

## 2. Diagnosis
- Widespread anterior ST elevation with chest pain suggests LAD occlusion. This is a type 1 MI or a type 2 MI with ST elevation (rarer).
- Differential: PE (right heart strain), aortic dissection, tamponade, pericarditis, takotsubo cardiomyopathy, coronary vasospasm, coronary embolus (air, paradoxical), and hyperkalaemia.
- Echo helps: anterior wall akinesia (LAD), RV dilation (PE), effusion (tamponade), aortic root and flap (dissection), and global dysfunction (takotsubo).
- Check for bleeding as a cause of hypotension and tachycardia.

## 3. Haemodynamic stabilisation
- BP 90/50 with a rate of 110 suggests low output or hypovolaemia.
- If hypovolaemia (bleeding, third spacing) is suspected, give small fluid or blood boluses of 250 mL, reassessing after each.
- If cardiogenic, avoid large volumes; use noradrenaline to maintain a MAP of at least 65, with dobutamine if low output persists after pressure is restored (see R8).
- Avoid nitrates while hypotensive.

## 4. Reperfusion strategy: the central decision
| Option | Considerations here |
|---|---|
| Primary PCI | The preferred strategy: door-to-device within 90 minutes (60 if already at a PCI centre). It does not need systemic fibrinolysis, and anticoagulation can be limited to the procedural dose. Femoral or radial access with a haemostasis plan |
| Fibrinolysis | Relatively or absolutely contraindicated by major surgery within 3 weeks (a 2-hour-old surgical wound with risk of haemorrhage, particularly after a prostatectomy). Reserve for situations where PCI is unavailable and the surgeon accepts the bleeding risk |
| CABG | Considered for left main or multivessel disease, or if PCI fails, with the cardiothoracic team |

Communicate with the surgeon about bleeding risk, haemostasis, and drains, and with the cardiologist about the stent choice (a bare-metal or newer DES with short DAPT may be chosen to reduce the duration of dual therapy, and balloon angioplasty alone may be used).

## 5. Antithrombotic therapy in a patient with a surgical wound
- **Aspirin:** 150 to 300 mg loading dose unless surgeon objection is overwhelming. It is the most important agent.
- **P2Y12 inhibitor and heparin:** usually given in the cath lab at the time of PCI; the choice and timing are agreed between cardiologist and surgeon. Options are clopidogrel (less potent, preferred where bleeding risk is high), cangrelor, or a lower heparin dose. GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors increase bleeding.
- Monitor the wound, haemoglobin, and drains.

## 6. Other management
- Beta-blocker only if there is no heart failure, shock or heart block; a high-intensity statin.
- Treat arrhythmias (VF, VT) according to ALS, and electrolytes (potassium above 4, magnesium above 1).
- Cardiogenic shock: see R8, with early consideration of MCS.
- Transfer to the cath lab, then CCU or ICU.

## 7. Priorities, in order
- Recognise and call for help.
- Stabilise haemodynamics and airway.
- Early primary PCI as the reperfusion therapy of choice.
- Minimise bleeding while giving the antithrombotic therapy that is essential.
- Detect and treat complications (shock, arrhythmia, mechanical).
- Communicate with the surgeon, patient and family.

> **Examiner lens:** reperfusion is the priority; explain why lytics are a poor choice after surgery.

items.q: State INR targets for prosthetic valves and the perioperative plan.
items.a:
- Mechanical aortic bileaflet without risk factors: INR 2.5 (2.0 to 3.0).
- Mechanical aortic with risk factors (AF, prior thromboembolism, LV dysfunction) or mitral/tricuspid: INR 3.0 (2.5 to 3.5).
- Bioprosthetic valve: aspirin (or warfarin for 3 to 6 months); DOACs are contraindicated in mechanical valves.
- Perioperative: stop warfarin 5 days before; bridge in high-risk patients (mechanical mitral, caged-ball, recent stroke); restart after haemostasis.
- Emergency reversal: vitamin K plus PCC.
- Pregnancy: see the trade-offs between warfarin and heparins.
- Endocarditis prophylaxis is relevant (see S29).

> **Closing point:** The valve position and type decide the thrombotic risk and the INR target.

items.sub: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.eyebrow: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.q: State the haemodynamic goals for anaesthesia in a patient with poor LV function.
items.a:
- Preload: normal to slightly high, avoid overload.
- Afterload: keep low to normal, but maintain MAP.
- Contractility: preserve or support.
- Heart rate: normal to slightly raised (stroke volume is fixed), avoid bradycardia.
- Rhythm: sinus.
- Ventilation: low PEEP and mean pressure, avoid hypoxia and hypercarbia.
- Monitoring: invasive BP, cardiac output, TOE.

> **Closing point:** Avoid anything that is a negative inotrope or raises afterload sharply.
