items.sub: 5. Acute pulmonary oedema
items.eyebrow: 5. Acute pulmonary oedema
items.q: Classify the causes of pulmonary oedema by mechanism.
items.a:
- Starling forces: raised hydrostatic pressure (cardiogenic, fluid overload, renal failure, valve disease, arrhythmia), lowered oncotic pressure (hypoalbuminaemia), raised permeability (ARDS, sepsis, aspiration, TRALI, pancreatitis, burns), lymphatic obstruction.
- Mixed: neurogenic oedema, high altitude, re-expansion, negative pressure (upper airway obstruction), post-obstructive, opioid overdose.
- Anaesthetic-specific: negative pressure after laryngospasm, TACO or TRALI, anaphylaxis, ischaemia, fluid overload, hypertension.
- Clues: speed of onset, BNP, echo, haemodynamic profile, fluid balance.

> **Closing point:** Classify by Starling force and treat the dominant mechanism.

items.title: 19. HCM: hypotension after induction
items.q: A 40-year-old with HCM becomes profoundly hypotensive after induction of general anaesthesia. Explain the mechanism, your treatment, and why ephedrine is a poor choice.
items.a:
## 1. Background: the physiology of HCM
- HCM is an autosomal dominant sarcomere disorder (MYH7, MYBPC3) with unexplained LV hypertrophy (wall thickness 15 mm or more), a small LV cavity, myocardial disarray, diastolic dysfunction, and microvascular ischaemia. About one-third have resting LVOT obstruction (gradient 30 mmHg or more) and another third have latent obstruction provoked by exercise or Valsalva.
- Dynamic LVOT obstruction arises from systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the anterior mitral valve leaflet, pulled into the outflow tract by the Venturi effect and drag as flow accelerates through a narrowed, abnormally positioned outflow tract. SAM also causes mitral regurgitation (posteriorly directed jet).

## 2. Why the patient is hypotensive after induction
The obstruction worsens with:

- **Reduced preload** (venodilation, fasting, bleeding): the cavity shrinks, bringing the septum and mitral valve closer.
- **Reduced afterload** (vasodilation from propofol or volatile): less pressure to keep the leaflet away from the septum, and a higher flow velocity.
- **Increased contractility** (sympathetic stimulation, inotropes) and **tachycardia** (shorter filling time).

Thus the hypotension from induction (loss of SVR and preload) increases obstruction, lowers stroke volume, and causes a downward spiral of hypotension, ischaemia and tachycardia.

## 3. Management of acute hypotension
- Call for help and confirm the diagnosis (look for other causes of hypotension: bleeding, anaphylaxis, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, arrhythmia, ischaemia, high spinal).
- Give a **pure alpha agonist** (phenylephrine 50 to 100 micrograms boluses, or an infusion; vasopressin 1 to 2 units) to restore SVR and afterload.
- Give a **fluid bolus** (250 to 500 mL crystalloid or colloid) to restore preload; elevate the legs.
- Reduce volatile concentration and treat pain/anaesthesia depth to reduce vasodilation.
- Slow tachycardia with esmolol (0.5 mg/kg then infusion) if BP has been restored; this prolongs diastolic filling and reduces contractility.
- TOE: look for SAM, LVOT gradient, MR, LV cavity size, and RWMA.
- Cardioversion for AF or haemodynamically significant arrhythmia (loss of atrial kick can precipitate collapse).

## 4. Why ephedrine and other inotropes are a poor choice
- Ephedrine has beta-1 effects (positive inotropy and chronotropy), which narrow the LVOT, increase SAM, and shorten diastolic filling.
- Adrenaline, dobutamine, dopamine, isoprenaline, and milrinone have the same effect and may precipitate haemodynamic collapse.
- Nitrates and other vasodilators lower afterload and preload and worsen the gradient.
- Large doses of volatile agents and propofol vasodilate and depress preload.
- Digoxin and other inotropes are also avoided.

## 5. Refractory hypotension
- Escalate vasopressor infusions (phenylephrine, vasopressin, noradrenaline), continue fluid, and use esmolol if tachycardic.
- Consider an arterial line, and check ABG, potassium and calcium.
- If there is still no response, consider VA-ECMO as a bridge (avoid IABP, which can increase obstruction), and call cardiology and ICU.
- CPR in HCM may be ineffective in the presence of obstruction; ensure the patient has pads on and an ICD interrogation plan.

## 6. Prevention
- Assess the risk preoperatively: symptoms, gradient (rest and Valsalva), MR, ICD, family history of sudden cardiac death, drugs (beta-blocker, verapamil, disopyramide, mavacamten).
- Continue beta-blockers, verapamil or disopyramide on the day.
- Avoid prolonged fasting; give IV fluid before induction.
- Insert an arterial line before induction, with a phenylephrine infusion prepared.
- Slow titrated induction with etomidate or reduced propofol and an opioid, avoid ketamine and pancuronium, maintain with volatile or TIVA titrated to avoid vasodilation.
- Neuraxial: slowly titrated epidural may be acceptable; avoid a single-shot spinal.
- ICD management (see R21).

> **Examiner lens:** explain by the dynamic obstruction (Venturi and SAM), not by memory.

items.title: 6. Cardiomyopathy
items.body:
## 6.1 Classification

| Type | Key features | Perioperative priority |
|---|---|---|
| Dilated (DCM) | LV dilatation, systolic dysfunction (EF below 40%); causes: idiopathic or familial, ischaemic, alcohol, viral, anthracycline, peripartum, tachycardia-induced, valvular | Treat as HFrEF (Topic 3) |
| Hypertrophic (HCM) | Unexplained LVH (wall 15 mm or more), diastolic dysfunction, myocyte disarray; autosomal dominant sarcomere mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3); dynamic LVOT obstruction in about 70% (rest or provoked) with systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve; SCD risk | **Examiner favourite**; avoid anything that reduces LV size or increases contractility or heart rate |
| Restrictive (RCM) | Stiff ventricle, normal EF, biatrial enlargement; amyloid, sarcoid, haemochromatosis, fibrosis, radiation | Preload-dependent, fixed low output, poor tolerance of tachycardia and AF |
| Arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy | RV fibrofatty replacement, VT | Arrhythmia risk; ICD |
| Takotsubo (stress) | Transient apical ballooning after catecholamine surge; mimics STEMI, normal coronaries | Can occur intraoperatively; supportive care, avoid catecholamines if LVOT obstruction |
| Peripartum | EF below 45% in last month of pregnancy or 5 months postpartum | See obstetrics sets |
| Ischaemic | Not truly a primary cardiomyopathy (CAD) | Topics 1 to 3 |
| Right heart failure | RV pressure or volume overload (pulmonary hypertension, PE, RV infarct) | See 6.6 |

## 6.2 Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy

**Pathophysiology:** asymmetric septal hypertrophy narrows the LV outflow tract. During systole, the Venturi effect and drag forces pull the anterior mitral leaflet toward the septum (SAM), worsening obstruction and causing posterior-directed MR. Obstruction is **dynamic**: it worsens with reduced LV volume (hypovolaemia, vasodilation), increased contractility (catecholamines, inotropes) and tachycardia, and reduced afterload. Diastolic dysfunction from LVH raises LVEDP, and myocardial oxygen supply-demand mismatch causes ischaemia despite normal coronaries.

| Factor | Increases obstruction | Decreases obstruction |
|---|---|---|
| Preload | Hypovolaemia, venodilation, PEEP, positioning (head up) | Volume loading, leg raise, head-down |
| Afterload | Vasodilation, low SVR | Vasoconstrictors (phenylephrine, vasopressin) |
| Contractility | Beta-agonists, dobutamine, ketamine, digoxin, calcium | Beta-blockers, verapamil, volatile agents, disopyramide |
| Heart rate | Tachycardia (shortens diastolic filling and LV size) | Slow rate |
| Rhythm | AF (loss of atrial kick, poor filling) | Sinus rhythm |

**Preoperative assessment:** symptoms (dyspnoea, angina, syncope, palpitation), family history of sudden death, ECG (LVH, strain, deep Q waves), echo (wall thickness, LVOT gradient at rest and with Valsalva, SAM, MR, diastolic function), cardiac MRI (fibrosis, late gadolinium enhancement), Holter monitoring, and review of medications (beta-blocker, verapamil, disopyramide, amiodarone). ICD in situ requires reprogramming (see Set 12). SCD risk markers: previous cardiac arrest, VT, family history, massive LVH (30 mm or more), unexplained syncope, NSVT, abnormal BP response, LVOT gradient above 30 mmHg.

**Perioperative haemodynamic goals:**

- **Preload:** full. Avoid prolonged fasting (maintain IV fluids), avoid venodilators and bowel prep dehydration; maintain preload with fluid or blood.
- **Afterload:** maintain or increase (phenylephrine, vasopressin, noradrenaline).
- **Contractility:** reduce (volatile anaesthetics, beta-blocker).
- **Rate:** low-normal (60 to 70), sinus rhythm (cardiovert early for AF; consider amiodarone).
- **Avoid:** ephedrine, adrenaline, dobutamine, isoprenaline, ketamine, tachycardia, hypovolaemia, and nitrates.

**Technique:**

| Element | Approach |
|---|---|
| Premedication | Continue beta-blocker or verapamil; anxiolysis (reduce catecholamines) |
| Monitoring | Arterial line before induction, ECG with ST, TOE if major surgery or instability, defibrillator pads, CVP of limited value |
| Induction | Slow, titrated propofol or etomidate with fentanyl, vasopressor infusion running (phenylephrine, metaraminol, vasopressin) |
| Maintenance | Volatile agent, opioid, remifentanil; avoid light anaesthesia and pain |
| Neuraxial | Not contraindicated, but sympathectomy lowers preload and afterload: use slow incremental epidural, CSE with low-dose spinal, or avoid; GA is more predictable in severe obstruction. In pregnancy epidural labour analgesia is acceptable with vasopressor cover |
| Hypotension post induction | **Do not give ephedrine or inotropes.** Treat with a pure alpha-agonist (phenylephrine 50 to 100 micrograms, or vasopressin), fluid bolus, reduce volatile concentration, leg elevation, and treat tachycardia (esmolol). Check for another cause (bleeding, anaphylaxis, tension pneumothorax, ischaemia, arrhythmia). If refractory: TOE to confirm SAM and LVOT obstruction, then vasoconstrictor infusions |
| Pneumoperitoneum (laparoscopic cholecystectomy) | Insufflation raises SVR (good), but decreased venous return in head-up (bad). Slow insufflation, low pressure, head-down tilt, fluid loading |
| Arrhythmia | Cardiovert unstable; amiodarone or beta-blocker for AF; do not use digoxin |
| Emergence | Avoid hypertension and tachycardia; extubate smoothly; ICU or HDU postoperative |

**Pregnancy, labour and delivery in HCM:** pregnancy changes that help: rising blood volume (40 to 50%) increases preload and enlarges the LV cavity, reducing the gradient. Changes that harm: falling SVR (more LVOT gradient), tachycardia and pain in labour, catecholamine surges, blood loss at delivery, and aortocaval compression. Principles: left lateral position, early slow-titrated epidural with a vasopressor ready, assisted second stage (avoid prolonged Valsalva), slow oxytocin infusion rather than a bolus (hypotension, tachycardia), avoid tocolytics and beta-agonists (tachycardia), and prompt volume replacement of haemorrhage.

**Alcohol septal ablation, myectomy, mavacamten (EXPLORER-HCM) and ICD** are the disease treatments: myectomy for refractory obstruction; mavacamten (cardiac myosin inhibitor) reduces gradient and improves functional class.

## 6.3 Dilated cardiomyopathy and low EF

Treat as severe LV systolic dysfunction (Topic 3), with attention to arrhythmia, devices and thromboembolism.

**Cardiac implantable devices (pacemaker, ICD, CRT) in cardiomyopathy:**

- **Preoperative:** identify the device, indication and pacing dependence; confirm a recent interrogation (about 12 months for a pacemaker, 6 months for an ICD or CRT) and the current programming. Review medications and the rhythm; echo and BNP if function has changed.
- **Electromagnetic interference:** monopolar diathermy above the umbilicus is the main risk. Use bipolar diathermy or short bursts, place the return pad so the current path avoids the generator, and monitor the pulse waveform (pulse oximeter or arterial line) because the ECG may be distorted.
- **Pacemaker:** a magnet usually produces asynchronous pacing; reprogram to asynchronous mode if the patient is pacemaker-dependent and interference is expected.
- **ICD:** a magnet usually suspends tachyarrhythmia therapies but does not alter pacing. Suspend therapies (magnet or programmer) when diathermy is expected, apply external defibrillation pads first, and have an external defibrillator ready. Restore therapies and re-interrogate before the patient leaves a monitored area.
- **CRT:** loss of biventricular capture reduces cardiac output; confirm capture and treat AF or ectopy that reduces pacing percentage.

**Choosing the anaesthetic technique in severe LV dysfunction:**

| Technique | Advantages | Risks and precautions |
|---|---|---|
| Regional or neuraxial (slow epidural, CSE with incremental local anaesthetic, peripheral nerve block) | Avoids airway instrumentation and positive pressure ventilation; reduces afterload; allows titrated onset | Hypotension from vasodilation (have a vasopressor infusion running, titrate slowly), fluid overload from preloading, and anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy limiting neuraxial use. Single-shot spinal gives abrupt sympathectomy and is riskier |
| General anaesthesia | Controlled airway and ventilation; suits instability, pulmonary oedema or failed block | Loss of sympathetic tone, myocardial depression with induction agents, pressor response to laryngoscopy, reduced venous return with positive pressure ventilation; use titrated induction with arterial monitoring |
| Sedation or local | Minimal haemodynamic disturbance for superficial surgery | Over-sedation with hypoventilation raises PVR and CO2; maintain monitoring |

**Alcohol and thiamine:** alcohol cardiomyopathy may improve with abstinence; give thiamine.

**Anthracycline cardiotoxicity (doxorubicin):** dose-related (cumulative above 450 to 550 mg/m2) and also trastuzumab; check baseline EF and troponin.

## 6.4 Restrictive cardiomyopathy and amyloidosis

- Stiff, non-compliant ventricles: small changes in volume cause large changes in pressure; fixed stroke volume depends on HR (avoid bradycardia); tolerate neither hypovolaemia nor fluid overload; AF is poorly tolerated.
- Amyloid (AL, ATTR): autonomic neuropathy (hypotension), conduction disease, thickened walls with low voltage ECG, and sensitivity to vasodilators and neuraxial block. Avoid digoxin and non-dihydropyridine CCB (bind amyloid fibrils).
- Goals: maintain preload and sinus rhythm, avoid bradycardia and vasodilation, titrate anaesthetic, and use vasopressors (phenylephrine, vasopressin).

## 6.5 Takotsubo and peripartum cardiomyopathy

**Takotsubo:** typically postmenopausal women, emotional or physical stress (includes surgery); chest pain and ST elevation, troponin mildly raised, apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis, normal angiography; 20% have LVOT obstruction (avoid catecholamines). Management: supportive, treat HF, anticoagulate if LV thrombus, MCS if shock; EF recovers in weeks.

**Peripartum cardiomyopathy:** EF below 45%, late pregnancy to 5 months postpartum; HF management with pregnancy-safe agents (beta-blocker, hydralazine, nitrate, diuretic, bromocriptine in selected cases); anticoagulate if EF below 35%; delivery planning.

## 6.6 Right heart failure and pulmonary hypertension (BT_PO 1.5 right heart failure component)

**Aetiology:** pulmonary hypertension (group 1 PAH; group 2 left heart disease; group 3 lung disease or hypoxia; group 4 CTEPH; group 5 multifactorial), RV infarction, PE, congenital shunt, cor pulmonale.

**Pathophysiology:** the RV is a thin-walled, compliant, volume-tolerant pump poorly adapted to high afterload. A rise in PVR dilates the RV, flattens the septum (ventricular interdependence), reduces LV filling, and lowers RV coronary perfusion, causing a vicious spiral of ischaemia, further failure and shock.

**Management principles (perioperative RV failure):**

| Principle | Actions |
|---|---|
| Preload | Avoid both hypovolaemia and overload; aim CVP 8 to 12 mmHg; diurese if overloaded |
| Afterload (PVR) | Avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia, pain, high airway pressures and PEEP; use inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (nitric oxide 20 ppm, inhaled epoprostenol), sildenafil, milrinone |
| Contractility | Dobutamine, milrinone, low-dose adrenaline; levosimendan |
| Perfusion pressure | Keep SBP above PASP; noradrenaline or vasopressin (vasopressin raises SVR with less effect on PVR) |
| Rhythm | Maintain sinus rhythm; cardiovert early |
| Mechanical | RVAD, VA-ECMO, atrial septostomy in selected |
| Anaesthetic | Avoid anything that increases PVR (nitrous oxide, N2O, ketamine in large doses, hypoventilation); neuraxial anaesthesia with care; aim for PVR down and SVR up |
| Monitoring | Arterial line, CVP, PA catheter or TOE (RV size, septal position, TAPSE, FAC) |

**Echo of RV function:** TAPSE below 17 mm, S' below 9.5 cm/s, FAC below 35%, RV:LV ratio above 1, septal flattening (D-sign), and PASP from TR velocity (PASP = 4 x v^2 + RAP).

items.title: Describe how echo grades diastolic dysfunction and estimates filling pressure.
items.sub: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.eyebrow: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.q: Describe how echo grades diastolic dysfunction and estimates filling pressure.
items.a:
- Measurements: mitral E and A velocities, E/A ratio, deceleration time, tissue Doppler e' (septal and lateral), E/e', LA volume index, TR velocity, pulmonary vein flow.
- Screening criteria: septal e' below 7 or lateral below 10 cm/s, average E/e' above 14, LAVI above 34 mL/m2, TR velocity above 2.8 m/s; more than half positive means dysfunction.
- Grade I: impaired relaxation, E/A below 0.8, normal filling pressure.
- Grade II: pseudonormal, E/A 0.8 to 2, E/e' 10 to 14, raised filling pressure; Valsalva unmasks.
- Grade III: restrictive, E/A above 2, short DT (below 160 ms), high filling pressure.
- Limits: AF, MR, mitral stenosis, annular calcification, tachycardia.

> **Closing point:** A pseudonormal pattern is the easiest to miss.

items.title: Describe the steps in managing acute decompensated heart failure.
items.sub: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.eyebrow: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.q: Describe the steps in managing acute decompensated heart failure.
items.a:
- Assess: ABC, SBP, perfusion, congestion (warm/cold, wet/dry).
- Oxygen and CPAP/NIV for hypoxia (3CPO); intubate if failing.
- Search for the cause: ACS, arrhythmia, hypertension, valve, infection, drugs, PE.
- Diuretic: IV furosemide at 1 to 2.5 times oral dose; add thiazide or acetazolamide if resistant.
- Vasodilator (GTN) if SBP above 110 and congestion.
- Low output or hypotension: noradrenaline, dobutamine or milrinone; MCS if refractory.
- Monitor: echo, lactate, renal function, urine output, weight.
- Prevent: restart GDMT before discharge.

> **Closing point:** Perfusion first, then congestion.

items.title: 9. Mechanical complications after MI
items.q: Three days after an inferior MI a patient develops pulmonary oedema and shock with a new murmur. How do you distinguish papillary muscle rupture from a ventricular septal rupture, and what is your immediate plan?
items.a:
## 1. Recognition and framing
- Mechanical complications occur in about 0.5 to 1% of MIs in the primary PCI era but account for up to 15% of MI deaths. They typically present 2 to 7 days after MI (earlier with fibrinolysis, and in anterior MI with a late presenter) with sudden haemodynamic deterioration, pulmonary oedema or shock and a new murmur.
- The differential for post-MI shock with a new murmur is: papillary muscle rupture (acute severe MR), ventricular septal rupture (VSR), and free wall rupture (usually tamponade rather than a murmur). Other causes of deterioration: re-infarction, RV infarct, arrhythmia, tamponade, and LVOT obstruction with SAM.

## 2. Distinguishing features
| Feature | Papillary muscle rupture (acute MR) | Ventricular septal rupture | Free wall rupture |
|---|---|---|---|
| Typical infarct | Inferior or posterior (posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply from the PDA); anterolateral muscle has dual supply | Anterior (apical septum, LAD) or inferior (basal septum, RCA) | Anterior or lateral, first MI, older women, hypertension, late reperfusion |
| Timing | 2 to 7 days | 3 to 5 days | Within 5 days (up to 2 weeks); acute (PEA) or subacute (pseudoaneurysm) |
| Murmur | Soft, short or absent (rapid pressure equalisation); apical pansystolic, may radiate to axilla | Loud harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge with a palpable thrill | Usually no murmur; muffled sounds, pulsus paradoxus |
| Exam | Pulmonary oedema, usually normal-sized heart | Biventricular failure, signs of RV overload | Tamponade (Beck's triad), PEA |
| Echo | Flail or prolapsing leaflet, severe eccentric MR jet, hyperdynamic LV with mild-to-moderate infarction | Defect in septum with left-to-right shunt on colour Doppler, RV dilation | Pericardial effusion with clot, tamponade, myocardial tear |
| PA catheter | High PCWP with giant v waves | Step-up in O2 saturation from RA to RV (more than 5% or 10%) | Equalised diastolic pressures |
| ECG | Variable | Variable, may show new bundle branch block or AV block | Variable |

## 3. Immediate management of papillary muscle rupture and VSR
- **Resuscitate** and move to a cardiac centre; call the cardiothoracic surgeon and cardiologist (heart team).
- **Confirm** with TTE or TOE, with the Doppler to quantify MR or shunt.
- **Reduce afterload and improve forward flow:**
- IABP, which is the most useful bridge in these conditions: reduces afterload and MR or left-to-right shunt, and raises coronary perfusion.
- Vasodilators if BP allows (sodium nitroprusside 0.3 to 5 micrograms/kg/min, GTN), with arterial monitoring.
- Inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone) and vasopressors if hypotensive; avoid raising SVR excessively.
- **Ventilation:** PEEP for pulmonary oedema in papillary rupture; in VSR, avoid high PVR (it increases the shunt if PVR falls, or conversely, high PVR reduces shunt, so balance).
- **Definitive treatment:** urgent surgery for papillary muscle rupture (mitral valve replacement, usually with a mechanical or bioprosthetic valve, or repair) and for VSR (patch repair; delay is considered in stable patients to allow scar formation, but most unstable patients need early surgery). Percutaneous options (transcatheter mitral edge-to-edge repair; septal occluder devices) are used for high-risk surgical candidates. ECMO or Impella may bridge selected cases.
- Mortality is very high (up to 40 to 90% medically), and timing is critical.

## 4. Anaesthetic considerations in these patients
- Arterial line and central access prior to induction, with the patient on a vasopressor and inotrope.
- Titrated induction with etomidate, ketamine or high-dose opioid, aiming for stable afterload (low SVR in MR and VSR improves forward flow), avoiding bradycardia (in MR), and avoiding large increases in PVR.
- TOE for diagnosis and for assessment after repair.

## 5. Free wall rupture
Pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage and emergency surgery. Support with fluid and vasopressors while preparing; avoid inotropes that increase wall stress.

## 6. Key learning points
- A new murmur with pulmonary oedema or shock after MI is a mechanical complication until proven otherwise.
- The murmur in papillary rupture can be soft; do not be reassured by its absence.

> **Examiner lens:** inferior MI, single blood supply and a soft murmur are the cue for papillary muscle rupture.

items.title: Compare IABP, Impella and VA-ECMO.
items.sub: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.eyebrow: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.q: Compare IABP, Impella and VA-ECMO.
items.a:
- IABP: counterpulsation, adds about 0.5 L/min, reduces afterload and improves coronary diastolic flow; needs a rhythm and some LV function; no mortality benefit in IABP-SHOCK II.
- Impella (microaxial pump): LV to aorta, 2.5 to 5.5 L/min, unloads the LV; complications: haemolysis, bleeding, limb ischaemia, aortic valve injury; DanGer Shock showed lower mortality in selected STEMI shock.
- VA-ECMO: full cardiopulmonary support (4 to 6 L/min), works in arrest and biventricular or respiratory failure; raises afterload, so LV distension and pulmonary oedema may require venting; complications: limb ischaemia, stroke, bleeding, differential hypoxaemia (Harlequin syndrome).
- Contraindications: severe AR (IABP, Impella), aortic dissection, LV thrombus (Impella), prosthetic aortic valve (Impella).
- Goal: bridge to recovery, device, transplant or decision.

> **Closing point:** Devices buy time, so know the exit strategy before insertion.

items.title: 15. Severe aortic stenosis for non-cardiac surgery
items.q: A 78-year-old with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis needs an urgent hemicolectomy. How do you assess, plan and manage the anaesthetic, and how would your approach differ from a patient with HCM?
items.a:
## 1. Pathophysiology
- Fixed LV outflow obstruction raises LV systolic pressure and wall stress, causing concentric hypertrophy. Hypertrophy increases oxygen demand and reduces compliance (diastolic dysfunction), while the shortened diastolic coronary filling and high LVEDP reduce supply. Subendocardial ischaemia occurs even with normal coronary arteries.
- Cardiac output is fixed across the valve: it cannot increase with demand, and any fall in preload, SVR or rate results in a fall in perfusion pressure and ischaemia. A vicious cycle of hypotension, ischaemia, falling contractility and further hypotension can follow.
- The stiff LV depends on atrial contraction (up to 40% of filling) and on adequate diastolic time.

## 2. Preoperative assessment
- **Symptoms:** angina, syncope, dyspnoea carry a high risk (median survival of 2 to 3 years once symptomatic without valve replacement).
- **Echo (within 12 months, earlier if symptoms change):** Vmax 4 m/s or more, mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, AVA below 1.0 cm2 (indexed below 0.6 cm2/m2), dimensionless index below 0.25; LV size, EF, wall thickness, associated MR, pulmonary pressure. Low-flow low-gradient AS (SVi below 35 mL/m2) may be underestimated.
- **Other:** ECG (LVH, strain, AF), BNP, coronary assessment when indicated (angiography or CT), renal function.
- **Perioperative risk:** severe AS carries a raised risk of death, MI and heart failure with non-cardiac surgery (about 3 to 10 times control in older series, lower in modern series with careful anaesthesia).

## 3. Decision-making
- Symptomatic severe AS: treat the valve first if the non-cardiac surgery can wait (SAVR or TAVI, PARTNER 3 and Evolut Low Risk demonstrating TAVI is non-inferior or superior to surgery in low risk patients; SAVR for those with surgical risk who are young or have bicuspid or root disease). TAVI also allows early (within weeks) non-cardiac surgery.
- Urgent surgery cannot wait: proceed with optimal anaesthesia; consider balloon valvuloplasty as a bridge (short-lived effect) in selected patients.
- Asymptomatic severe AS with elevated-risk surgery: proceed with careful technique and monitoring (shared decision).
- Multidisciplinary discussion including cardiology and surgeons, with documentation of the discussion with the patient.

## 4. Anaesthetic goals and technique
| Goal | Why | How |
|---|---|---|
| Heart rate 60 to 80 | Long ejection and diastolic filling times | Avoid tachycardia (pain, light anaesthesia, pancuronium, ketamine), treat bradycardia (preserve CO) |
| Sinus rhythm | Atrial kick | Treat AF immediately with synchronised cardioversion; amiodarone for rate; pads on |
| Preload full | Stiff LV | Careful fluid titration; avoid overload |
| SVR and MAP maintained | Coronary perfusion of a hypertrophied ventricle | Phenylephrine, noradrenaline, vasopressin; infusion running before induction |
| Contractility preserved | Needed to overcome the obstruction | Avoid high-dose volatile or myocardial depressants |

- **Monitoring:** arterial line before induction; ECG with ST analysis; consider TOE and cardiac output monitoring for major surgery; defibrillator pads in place (resuscitation is rarely successful in severe AS).
- **Induction:** slow titrated induction with etomidate or a reduced dose of propofol with an opioid, and a vasopressor infusion in place.
- **Neuraxial:** avoid single-shot spinal (abrupt vasodilation); slow epidural or CSE with low-dose may be used by experienced practitioners, with a vasopressor ready.
- **Hypotension:** treat early and aggressively with alpha agonists and volume, not by waiting. Avoid vasodilators and large volumes of nitrates.
- **Postoperative:** HDU, troponin, restrained analgesia, avoid hypotension and tachycardia, careful fluids.

## 5. Contrast with HCM
| Feature | Aortic stenosis | HCM |
|---|---|---|
| Obstruction | Fixed (valvular) | Dynamic (SAM and septal hypertrophy) |
| Heart rate | Slow-normal (60 to 80) | Slow (50 to 70) |
| Preload | Full | Full, even supranormal, to enlarge the LV cavity |
| Afterload | Maintain | Maintain or raise (alpha-agonists) |
| Contractility | Preserve | Reduce (beta-blocker, volatile); avoid inotropes |
| Inotropes | Cautious use for low output | Avoid; ephedrine, dobutamine and adrenaline worsen the gradient |
| Vasodilators | Avoid | Avoid |

The unifying principles are full preload, slow rate, sinus rhythm and maintained afterload; the difference is that increasing contractility helps in AS and harms in HCM.

> **Examiner lens:** show you understand the common LVH physiology and the single key difference.

items.title: Distinguish primary from secondary MR and give the haemodynamic goals.
items.sub: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.eyebrow: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.q: Distinguish primary from secondary MR and give the haemodynamic goals.
items.a:
- Primary: leaflet or chordal disease (prolapse, flail, rheumatic, endocarditis); secondary (functional): LV dilation from ischaemic or dilated cardiomyopathy.
- Acute MR (papillary rupture, endocarditis) causes pulmonary oedema and shock; chronic MR compensates with a large LA.
- Severity: vena contracta 7 mm or more, effective regurgitant orifice 0.4 cm2 or more, regurgitant volume 60 mL or more, pulmonary vein systolic reversal.
- Goals: heart rate normal to high-normal (80 to 90; bradycardia increases regurgitation), preload maintained, low afterload (vasodilators help), contractility supported.
- Avoid raised PVR and bradycardia.
- Pitfall: MR masks LV dysfunction, because EF is overestimated; EF below 60% implies significant dysfunction.

> **Closing point:** A fast, vasodilated, full heart promotes forward flow.

items.title: Who needs antibiotic prophylaxis for endocarditis, and for what procedures?
items.sub: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.eyebrow: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.q: Who needs antibiotic prophylaxis for endocarditis, and for what procedures?
items.a:
- High-risk patients: prosthetic valve or material used for repair, previous endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, repaired congenital disease with residual shunt, cardiac transplant with valvulopathy.
- Procedures: dental procedures that manipulate gingiva or periapical region or perforate mucosa.
- Not routinely for GI, GU, respiratory or skin procedures unless infection is present (then cover the likely organism).
- Agent: amoxicillin 2 g oral (or ampicillin IV) 30 to 60 minutes before; clindamycin avoided now or replaced with cefalexin or azithromycin in allergy.
- Rationale: bacteraemia from daily activity is the larger cause; oral hygiene matters most.

> **Closing point:** Prophylaxis is for high-risk patients undergoing dental procedures only.

items.title: 22. RV failure and pulmonary hypertension in valve or cardiomyopathy disease
items.q: A patient with severe mitral regurgitation and pulmonary hypertension develops acute RV failure after induction. Explain the physiology and your management.
items.a:
## 1. RV physiology
- The RV is a thin-walled, compliant chamber ejecting into a low-resistance, high-compliance pulmonary circulation. It handles volume well, but poorly tolerates acute increases in afterload. Perfusion of the RV occurs in both systole and diastole (RCA), so it is vulnerable when systemic pressure falls or PA pressure rises.
- With a sudden rise in PVR, the RV dilates, the tricuspid annulus dilates (TR), the septum shifts toward the LV (ventricular interdependence), LV filling and output fall, and systemic hypotension reduces RV coronary perfusion pressure, creating a vicious cycle of ischaemia and failure.
- Pulmonary hypertension from left heart disease (mitral regurgitation, post-capillary) raises pressure chronically, and the RV may be near its limit. Any additional insult (hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, positive pressure ventilation, pain, protamine, nitrous oxide) can tip it into acute failure.

## 2. Recognition
- Hypotension, rising CVP, falling ETCO2 (low output), tachycardia, desaturation, arrhythmia, ST changes in inferior leads.
- TOE: dilated RV (RV:LV area ratio above 0.6 to 1), septal flattening or D-shaped LV, reduced TAPSE (below 16 mm), RV S' (below 10 cm/s), FAC below 35%, severe TR, dilated IVC, and pericardial effusion.
- PA catheter or CVP: CVP above PAOP or equal, PA pressures, and calculated PVR (PVR = (mPAP - PAOP)/CO, normal below 2 Wood units).

## 3. Management
| Aim | Interventions |
|---|---|
| Reverse triggers that raise PVR | 100% oxygen, ensure adequate ventilation, treat hypercarbia and acidosis (target PaCO2 of 35 to 40 mmHg and pH above 7.35), avoid hypothermia, treat pain and light anaesthesia, avoid nitrous oxide and excess PEEP, use low tidal volumes with limited plateau pressure, avoid atelectasis and lung overinflation |
| Pulmonary vasodilators | Inhaled nitric oxide (10 to 40 ppm) or inhaled epoprostenol (10 to 50 ng/kg/min) reduce PVR without systemic hypotension; IV milrinone (also inotropic, but vasodilates systemically); sildenafil; IV prostacyclins (cause systemic hypotension) |
| Support RV perfusion | Noradrenaline or vasopressin to maintain systemic pressure above PA pressure (target MAP above 65 to 70 or higher); avoid hypotension; vasopressin reduces the PVR:SVR ratio |
| Optimise preload | Aim for a CVP of 8 to 12 mmHg; a bolus of 250 mL if the RV is hypovolaemic; avoid overload (septal shift worsens LV filling); diurese or renal replacement if distended |
| Contractility | Dobutamine (2 to 10 micrograms/kg/min) or milrinone; adrenaline for refractory cases; levosimendan |
| Rhythm | Keep sinus rhythm (atrial contribution), cardiovert AF or flutter early; treat bradycardia |
| Mechanical support | RVAD (Impella RP, ProtekDuo), VA-ECMO if refractory; bridge to recovery, surgery or transplant |
| Treat the cause | PE (thrombolysis or embolectomy), RV infarct (reperfusion), valve repair, ARDS (lung-protective strategy, prone), LVAD-associated RV failure |

## 4. Mitral regurgitation and left-sided considerations
- Severe MR with pulmonary hypertension: maintain a moderate heart rate (80 to 90), avoid bradycardia, reduce afterload, and keep preload adequate.
- Treat pulmonary venous hypertension (diuretic, inodilator) to lower the PA pressure.
- Pulmonary hypertension from left heart disease tends to respond poorly to pulmonary vasodilators and may cause pulmonary oedema if used without addressing the left-sided problem.

## 5. Anaesthetic prevention
- Avoid induction in poorly controlled pulmonary hypertension without preparation: arterial line, central venous access, TOE, vasopressor and inotrope prepared, and inhaled vasodilator available.
- Maintain spontaneous ventilation where possible, or use gentle ventilation with low PEEP.
- Avoid ketamine at high doses in severe pulmonary hypertension (may raise PVR), and avoid hypoxia and hypercarbia during induction and emergence.

## 6. Summary
The RV needs perfusion pressure, optimised preload, contractility and a lower PVR. Treat the cause, support systemic pressure first, and use pulmonary vasodilators and inotropes to break the cycle.

> **Examiner lens:** raise coronary perfusion and lower PVR; the RV needs pressure, not volume.

items.title: 12. HFpEF versus HFrEF: contrasting haemodynamic goals
items.q: Contrast the preferred perioperative haemodynamic goals for a patient with systolic dysfunction and a patient with diastolic dysfunction, and explain the physiology behind the differences.
items.a:
## 1. Background physiology
- **Systolic dysfunction (HFrEF):** reduced contractility and a dilated LV with a flat Starling curve. Stroke volume is low and fixed, so cardiac output depends on heart rate and on adequate preload without overload. The failing ventricle is sensitive to afterload (SV falls steeply with increased afterload) and to negative inotropes.
- **Diastolic dysfunction (HFpEF):** stiff, hypertrophied LV with impaired relaxation and compliance, and a steep end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship. Normal EF but raised filling pressures. Filling depends on time (heart rate), atrial contraction (up to 30 to 40% of stroke volume) and preload, and small volume changes cause large pressure changes.
- Both groups tolerate ischaemia poorly, and both may coexist.

## 2. Contrast of goals
| Goal | Systolic dysfunction (HFrEF) | Diastolic dysfunction (HFpEF, LVH) |
|---|---|---|
| Heart rate | Normal to high-normal (70 to 90); avoid bradycardia because stroke volume is fixed | Slow to normal (50 to 80) for long diastolic filling and coronary perfusion |
| Rhythm | Maintain sinus; treat AF with amiodarone or cardioversion; avoid new AF | Sinus rhythm critical (atrial kick); cardiovert early |
| Preload | Maintain but avoid overload; the ventricle is on the flat part of the curve | Maintain high-normal; hypovolaemia and hypervolaemia both lead to large changes in pressure |
| Afterload | Low to normal (vasodilatation helps forward flow), keeping MAP adequate | Avoid sudden rises (LVH, wall stress); maintain perfusion pressure to the hypertrophied myocardium |
| Contractility | Support: inotropes if low output; avoid negative inotropes (high-dose volatile, beta-blockade acutely) | Preserve; avoid excessive inotropy and tachycardia |
| Ventilation | Low mean airway pressures; PEEP reduces preload and afterload (can help) | Avoid hypercarbia, high pressures |
| Avoid | Vasoconstriction, bradycardia, myocardial depressants | Tachycardia, AF, hypotension, ischaemia, fluid overload |
| Monitoring | Arterial line, cardiac output, TOE | Arterial line, TOE for filling and function |

## 3. Drug choices
- Systolic dysfunction: etomidate or ketamine induction in titrated dose, opioid-based technique, low-dose volatile, vasopressors (noradrenaline, vasopressin), inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone, adrenaline), vasodilators for afterload reduction if the pressure allows.
- Diastolic dysfunction: keep a slow heart rate (esmolol, volatile, opioid, dexmedetomidine), vasopressors with minimal chronotropy (phenylephrine, vasopressin), fluids titrated to dynamic indices, early treatment of AF.

## 4. Linking to other lesions
The hypertrophied, stiff LV in aortic stenosis and HCM shares the diastolic goals (see R15 and R19). Reduced EF with MR or AR requires afterload reduction and a faster heart rate.

## 5. Practical rules
- Know the echo findings before the case (EF, E/e', LV thickness, valves, RV function).
- Prepare a vasopressor and an inotrope in each case.
- Treat the physiology rather than the number: a heart rate of 90 may help in HFrEF with MR, but may be harmful in HFpEF with AS.

> **Examiner lens:** link each goal to the underlying pressure-volume behaviour.

items.title: Describe the coronary arteries, the territories they supply, and the echo views that show them.
items.sub: 7. Heart and great vessel anatomy for ultrasound imaging
items.eyebrow: 7. Heart and great vessel anatomy for ultrasound imaging
items.q: Describe the coronary arteries, the territories they supply, and the echo views that show them.
items.a:
- Left main splits into LAD (anterior wall, anterior two-thirds of septum, apex) and circumflex (lateral wall, posterior wall in left-dominant hearts).
- RCA: RV, inferior wall, posterior third of septum (via PDA in right-dominant hearts, about 85%), SA node (60%) and AV node (80%).
- Territories on the 17-segment model: anterior and anteroseptal LAD; anterolateral and inferolateral LCx; inferior and inferoseptal RCA.
- Echo views: TOE mid-oesophageal four-chamber, two-chamber and long axis; transgastric mid short-axis shows all three territories; TTE parasternal long and short axis, apical four-, three- and two-chamber.
- RWMA scoring: normal, hypokinetic, akinetic, dyskinetic.
- Link: new RWMA on TOE appears before ECG changes.

> **Closing point:** The transgastric mid short-axis is the best single view to monitor ischaemia in all territories.

items.title: 20. Cardiomyopathy classification and anaesthetic implications
items.q: Compare dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive and takotsubo cardiomyopathy in terms of physiology, haemodynamic goals and anaesthetic pitfalls.
items.a:
## 1. Definition and classification
Cardiomyopathy is a disorder of the myocardium with structural and functional abnormality in the absence of coronary disease, hypertension, valve disease or congenital heart disease sufficient to cause the abnormality (ESC 2008; AHA 2006 classify by genetic or acquired causes). Phenotypes: dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive, arrhythmogenic right ventricular, and unclassified (including takotsubo and non-compaction).

## 2. Comparison
| Feature | Dilated (DCM) | Hypertrophic (HCM) | Restrictive (RCM) | Takotsubo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Causes | Idiopathic and genetic (titin), alcohol, viral, peripartum, chemotherapy (anthracycline), tachycardia-induced, iron overload, thyroid disease | Autosomal dominant sarcomere mutation; sometimes Fabry or Friedreich | Amyloid, sarcoid, haemochromatosis, radiation, endomyocardial fibrosis, scleroderma | Emotional or physical stress; catecholamine surge; postmenopausal women; subarachnoid haemorrhage; phaeochromocytoma |
| Haemodynamics | Dilated LV, low EF, high filling pressures, secondary MR, RV failure | Small LV cavity, hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, dynamic LVOT obstruction, MR | Stiff ventricles with small cavity, normal or mildly reduced EF, high filling pressures, fixed stroke volume, atrial enlargement | Apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis, reduced EF (recovers in 4 to 8 weeks), possible LVOT obstruction |
| Echo | Dilated, globally hypokinetic, thin walls | LVH, SAM, asymmetric septal hypertrophy | Thick walls (amyloid sparkling), biatrial dilation, restrictive filling (E/A above 2, short DT) | Apical akinesia and ballooning; no coronary territory pattern |
| ECG | LBBB, AF, ventricular ectopy | LVH, deep Q waves, T wave inversion | Low voltage (amyloid), AF, conduction disease | ST elevation or T wave inversion mimicking MI |
| Risk | Heart failure, arrhythmia, thromboembolism, sudden death | Sudden death (VT/VF), AF, HF, outflow obstruction | Heart failure, AF, thromboembolism | Heart failure, shock, arrhythmia, LVOT obstruction |
| Anaesthetic goals | Treat as HFrEF: maintain preload, afterload low-normal, support contractility, normal heart rate, sinus rhythm; low-dose induction; arterial line, cardiac output monitoring | Full preload, slow heart rate, sinus rhythm, maintain afterload, avoid inotropes and vasodilators (R19) | Maintain preload and heart rate (stroke volume is fixed), avoid bradycardia, vasodilation and tachycardia, treat AF early, avoid negative inotropes | Supportive; inotropes for shock if there is no obstruction, otherwise fluids and beta-blocker; mechanical support if refractory |
| Pitfalls | Sensitivity to induction agents, arrhythmia, LV thrombus, ICD/CRT | Ephedrine, hypovolaemia, tachycardia, high-dose volatile | Amyloid autonomic neuropathy (hypotension), digoxin and calcium channel blockers toxicity, difficult positive pressure ventilation | Catecholamine administration may worsen; recurrence |

## 3. Perioperative principles for all
- Preoperative echo and ECG, review of medications and any ICD or pacemaker (see R21), assessment of functional capacity, and consideration of a high-risk pathway.
- Arterial line before induction; invasive monitoring and TOE when appropriate.
- Anticipate arrhythmia and have pads on; correct potassium and magnesium.
- Anticoagulation in AF or LV thrombus is managed per guidelines.
- Postoperative HDU monitoring.

## 4. Key message
Decide whether the physiology is dilated, obstructed or stiff, then apply the matching goals; the pitfalls arise when a dilated-heart strategy (inotropes, vasodilators) is applied to an obstructed or stiff heart.

> **Examiner lens:** know the one-line physiology and the one key avoidance for each.

items.title: Classify cardiomyopathies and give a cause for each group.
items.sub: 6. Cardiomyopathy
items.eyebrow: 6. Cardiomyopathy
items.q: Classify cardiomyopathies and give a cause for each group.
items.a:
- Dilated: genetic (titin), alcohol, viral myocarditis, peripartum, chemotherapy (anthracycline), tachycardia-induced.
- Hypertrophic: sarcomere mutations (autosomal dominant), dynamic LVOT obstruction in about one-third.
- Restrictive: amyloid, sarcoid, haemochromatosis, endomyocardial fibrosis, radiation.
- Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy: desmosomal mutations, RV fatty replacement, VT.
- Takotsubo (stress) and peripartum.
- Ischaemic and secondary causes are classed separately.
- Common anaesthetic risks: arrhythmia, sudden death, thromboembolism, heart failure.

> **Closing point:** Identify the physiology, whether dilated, obstructed or stiff, then apply the matching goals.

items.title: Severe aortic stenosis presenting for hip fracture repair
items.source: Example drafted by Claude from the Set 11 chapter 4 notes. Check against your own sources.
items.q: An 82-year-old woman with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (mean gradient 48 mmHg, valve area 0.7 cm2, peak velocity 4.3 m/s) has a fractured neck of femur and needs surgery within 24 hours. Outline your anaesthetic management.
items.model:
## Assessment and timing

- Severe symptomatic AS is a **fixed-output state**: stroke volume cannot rise, so cardiac output depends on heart rate and rhythm. Pathophysiology: concentric LVH, raised LVEDP and wall tension, and subendocardial ischaemia from low DBP and high LVEDP even with normal coronaries.
- Elective surgery would be deferred until the valve is treated, but a hip fracture is urgent, so proceed. Discuss the high risk with the patient, family, surgeon, cardiologist and geriatrician, and document consent.
- Check symptoms (angina, syncope, heart failure), rhythm, ECG, recent echo, BNP, renal function, and haemoglobin.

## Haemodynamic goals

- **Avoid the three killers:** hypotension, tachycardia, and loss of sinus rhythm.
- HR 60 to 80, sinus rhythm, MAP at or above baseline (65 to 70 mmHg minimum), euvolaemia to slightly full, SVR maintained, contractility preserved.

## Plan

- Defibrillator pads on before induction. Invasive arterial line before induction. Consider TOE if instability.
- Vasopressor first (phenylephrine, metaraminol or noradrenaline), with a pre-emptive infusion running. Avoid pure vasodilators.
- GA with controlled induction and slow titration. Avoid a single-shot spinal (rapid sympathectomy). A slow epidural, CSE or low-dose spinal with vasopressor infusion has been used in selected cases.
- Treat AF or SVT with early synchronised cardioversion.
- Regional analgesia (for example a fascia iliaca block) reduces opioid and haemodynamic burden.

## Afterwards

HDU postoperatively. If the surgery were not urgent, balloon valvuloplasty or TAVI would be considered first.

Recognises urgency: proceeds rather than deferring, with documented risk discussion and multidisciplinary input

Names the three killers: hypotension, tachycardia, loss of sinus rhythm
Arterial line before induction and defibrillator pads on
